families.name: Hindu
families.note: About 1.2 billion Hindus, 14.9% of the world (Pew, 2020)

families.name: Modern and secular
families.note: About 24% of the world is religiously unaffiliated (Pew, 2020)

anim.name: Animism
anim.desc: Spirits live in animals, plants, places and natural forces.
anim.note: Probably the oldest layer of religion; inferred for Paleolithic hunter-gatherers and still central to many Indigenous traditions.

poly.name: Polytheism
poly.desc: Many gods with distinct roles and personalities.
poly.note: Typical of early cities and states (Sumer, Egypt, Vedic India, Greece), where gods were tied to cities, crafts and natural powers.

heno.name: Chief god among many
heno.desc: One god is supreme or worshipped exclusively, without denying that others exist (henotheism or monolatry).
heno.note: Seen in Marduk's rise in Babylon, early Israelite Yahweh worship and Hindu sects devoted to one deity.

mono.name: Monotheism
mono.note: Akhenaten's Aten cult (14th c. BCE) is the earliest attempt on record; it took lasting hold in Second Temple Judaism and passed to Christianity and Islam, with separate developments in Sikhism and elsewhere.

trin.name: Plural persons in one God
trin.desc: One God in several persons or aspects, such as the Christian Trinity.
trin.note: Defined for Christianity at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381); somewhat parallel triads appear in Hindu Trimurti thought and some Shia-derived groups.

mons.name: Monism or pantheism
mons.desc: All reality is ultimately one divine principle, or God and the universe are identical.
mons.note: Arises independently in the Upanishads (Brahman–Atman), Stoicism (Logos), Daoism and Neoplatonism (the One).

nont.name: Non-theistic
nont.desc: No creator God is central. Gods may exist but are not the point, or are rejected outright.
nont.note: Early Buddhism, Jainism and Cārvāka (c. 6th–5th c. BCE) are the classic cases; modern secular humanism is another.

sky.name: Sky father or distant high god
sky.desc: A supreme creator, often linked to the sky, who may be remote from daily life.
sky.note: Reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European religion (*Dyēus) and widespread in Africa, Siberia and the Americas.

fem.name: Goddess or divine feminine
fem.desc: Major female deities, a mother goddess, or a female aspect of the divine.
fem.note: Female figurines date back to the Upper Paleolithic, though what they meant is debated. Clear goddess cults appear in Sumer (Inanna), Egypt (Isis) and Hindu Shaktism.

ance.name: Ancestor veneration
ance.desc: The dead of the family or clan are honored, fed and consulted.
ance.note: Neolithic families buried their dead under house floors (Jericho, Çatalhöyük). Ancestor veneration is central in China, Africa and Oceania.

ang.name: Angels or intermediary spirits
ang.desc: Messengers or ranks of spirits between God and humans.
ang.note: Zoroastrian amesha spentas and yazatas likely shaped Second Temple Jewish angelology, which passed to Christianity and Islam.

devl.name: A devil or cosmic adversary
devl.desc: A chief evil being opposed to God.
devl.note: Angra Mainyu in Zoroastrianism is the earliest clear case; Satan becomes an adversary figure in Second Temple Judaism.

sain.name: Saints and holy persons
sain.desc: Holy people are venerated, often at shrines, and asked to intercede.
sain.note: Christian martyr cults (2nd c.), Sufi saints (walis), bodhisattvas and Jewish tzaddikim are parallel developments.

inc.name: Divine incarnation
inc.desc: God or a god takes human form (avatar, incarnation, living god).
inc.note: Pharaohs were identified with Horus. Hindu avatar doctrine and the Christian Incarnation developed separately, and later movements (Druze, Rastafari) added their own forms.

king.name: Sacred kingship
king.desc: Rulers are divine, descended from gods, or rule by heavenly mandate.
king.note: Universal in early states: Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Shang–Zhou Mandate of Heaven, the Inca, Hawaiʻi and imperial Japan.

crwt.name: Creation from primordial waters or chaos
crwt.desc: The world emerges from watery chaos or a formless void.
crwt.note: Found in Egypt (Nun), Mesopotamia (Tiamat), Genesis 1, the Vedas and Polynesia; probably among the oldest shared cosmogonies.

crex.name: Creation from nothing
crex.desc: God creates the universe out of nothing (ex nihilo).
crex.note: Formalized in Jewish and Christian theology around the 2nd c. CE and adopted by Islam.

demi.name: Flawed or lesser creator
demi.desc: The material world was made by an ignorant or evil lesser god (a demiurge).
demi.note: Distinctive of 2nd-century Gnosticism and Marcion. It was carried on by Manichaeans, Paulicians, Bogomils and Cathars.

cycl.name: Cyclical time
cycl.desc: The cosmos passes through repeating ages of creation and destruction.
cycl.note: Hindu–Buddhist–Jain kalpas and yugas, Maya and Aztec world ages, and the Stoic world-conflagration.

lin.name: Linear history toward an end
lin.desc: Time runs once, from creation to a final goal.
lin.note: Usually traced to Zoroastrianism, then Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

apoc.name: Apocalypse or end-times
apoc.desc: A coming final battle, judgment or transformation of the world.
apoc.note: Zoroastrian frashokereti, Jewish apocalyptic writing (Daniel, c. 165 BCE), Norse Ragnarök and many modern millennial movements.

mess.name: Coming savior or messiah
mess.desc: A future redeemer figure will restore the world.
mess.note: Zoroastrian Saoshyant, the Jewish Messiah, the Islamic Mahdi, Buddhist Maitreya and Kalki in Hinduism.

fate.name: Predestination or fate
fate.desc: Everything, including salvation, is fixed in advance.
fate.note: Ājīvika niyati (5th c. BCE), Islamic qadar, Calvinist predestination.

ordr.name: Cosmic moral order
ordr.desc: An impersonal law or order underlies nature and ethics.
ordr.note: Egyptian Ma'at, Vedic ṛta, Avestan aša, Greek Logos, Chinese Dao and Indian dharma.

dual.name: Cosmic dualism
dual.desc: The universe is a struggle between good and evil, or light and darkness.
dual.note: Zoroastrianism is the classic source; radical forms appear in Manichaeism, Gnosticism and Catharism.

axis.name: World tree or cosmic axis
axis.desc: A sacred tree, mountain or pillar links the heavens, earth and underworld.
axis.note: Norse Yggdrasil, the Maya ceiba, Mount Meru and the Siberian shamanic world tree.

flood.name: Great flood myth
flood.desc: A divine flood destroys most of humanity.
flood.note: The earliest texts are Mesopotamian (Ziusudra, Atrahasis, Gilgamesh). Flood stories also appear in Genesis, India (Manu), Greece and the Americas.

soul.name: Immortal individual soul
soul.desc: A lasting personal soul outlives the body.
soul.note: Egyptian ka/ba, Orphic and Platonic psyche, Indian ātman and Jain jīva.

anat.name: No permanent self
anat.desc: There is no unchanging self or soul (anattā).

matr.name: No afterlife (materialism)
matr.desc: Death is the end of the person.
matr.note: Cārvāka in India and Epicureanism in Greece; modern secular humanism.

undw.name: Shadowy underworld
undw.desc: All the dead go to a dim realm regardless of their deeds.
undw.note: Mesopotamian Kur, Hebrew Sheol, Greek Hades, Norse Hel.

judg.name: Judgment of the dead
judg.desc: Each person is judged after death on their deeds.
judg.note: The Egyptian weighing of the heart (by c. 2000 BCE) is the earliest clear case. Zoroastrianism has the Chinvat bridge.

hevh.name: Heaven and hell
hevh.note: Zoroastrian, then Jewish apocalyptic, Christian and Islamic; also Buddhist and Hindu heavens and hells within rebirth.

resu.name: Bodily resurrection
resu.desc: The dead will rise in bodies at the end of time.
resu.note: Zoroastrianism and Second Temple Judaism (Daniel 12), then Christianity and Islam.

rein.name: Rebirth or reincarnation
rein.desc: The self or a stream of consciousness is reborn in new bodies.
rein.note: Arises in the Upanishads and Śramaṇa movements around the 8th–6th c. BCE, and separately in Orphism and Pythagoreanism; also in Druze, Yoruba and Igbo traditions.

karm.name: Karma
karm.desc: Actions bring morally matching results in this or future lives.
karm.note: First stated in the Upanishads (c. 7th–6th c. BCE); central to Buddhism, Jainism, Hinduism and Sikhism.

libr.name: Liberation from rebirth
libr.desc: The goal is escape from the cycle of rebirth (moksha, nirvana, mukti).
libr.note: Śramaṇa and Upanishadic India, c. 6th c. BCE.

grac.name: Salvation by grace or faith
grac.desc: Salvation comes as a gift through faith or devotion, not by merit.
grac.note: Pauline Christianity, Lutheran sola fide, Pure Land trust in Amitābha, and Vaishnava devotional surrender.

grav.name: Burial with grave goods
grav.desc: The dead are buried with objects, food or companions for the next life.
grav.note: Among the oldest religious behavior: Middle Paleolithic burials with ochre (c. 100,000 years ago).

core.name: Core prohibitions
core.desc: A basic code against murder, theft, lying and sexual wrongdoing (Ten Commandments, Five Precepts, yamas).
core.note: Nearly universal; early codified forms include Egyptian Book of the Dead 'negative confessions' and Mesopotamian law.

gold.name: The Golden Rule
gold.desc: Treat others as you want to be treated.
gold.note: Confucius (Analects 15.24), the Mahābhārata, Buddhist texts, Hillel, Jesus and Islamic hadith; it arose independently many times.

dcmd.name: Morality as divine command
dcmd.desc: Moral law is commanded by God and revealed.
dcmd.note: Israelite covenant law, later Christianity and Islam; compare Hammurabi's code given by Shamash.

comp.name: Universal compassion
comp.desc: Love and compassion are owed to all beings, even enemies.
comp.note: Buddhist mettā/karuṇā, Mohist impartial care, Jesus's love of enemies, the Mahāyāna bodhisattva vow.

ahim.name: Non-violence to living beings
ahim.desc: Harming any living thing is wrong (ahiṃsā).
ahim.note: Śramaṇa India: Jainism carries it to an extreme, and Buddhism and Hinduism share it.

paci.name: Pacifism
paci.desc: Refusal to take part in war or violence.
paci.note: Jainism, early Christianity (debated), Anabaptists, Quakers, Mohists on offensive war, Doukhobors.

char.name: Obligatory charity
char.desc: Giving to the poor is a religious duty (zakat, tzedakah, dāna, langar).
char.note: Widespread; formalized in Judaism, Islam, Buddhism and Sikhism.

hosp.name: Sacred hospitality
hosp.desc: Guests and strangers are under divine protection.
hosp.note: Reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European (Greek xenia); strong in Semitic and Bedouin ethics.

just.name: Justice for the poor
just.desc: The faith demands justice for the poor, the widow and the oppressed.
just.note: Israelite prophets (Amos, 8th c. BCE), Islam, Sikhism, Mazdakism and modern liberation movements.

fili.name: Filial piety
fili.desc: Duty and reverence toward parents and elders as a central virtue.
fili.note: Zhou and Confucian China; spread across East Asia.

virt.name: Virtue cultivation
virt.desc: Ethics as cultivating character and harmony rather than following rules.
virt.note: Confucian ren, Daoist wu wei, Stoic and Aristotelian virtue, Buddhist pāramitās.

pure.name: Purity, pollution & taboo
pure.desc: Ritual cleanliness, impurity and forbidden things (tapu, kapu, fady).
pure.note: Universal; elaborated in Hindu, Zoroastrian, Jewish, Shinto and Polynesian systems.

land.name: Sacred land and kinship with nature
land.desc: Particular lands, waters and creatures are kin or holy.
land.note: Central to Aboriginal Australian, Indigenous American and Māori religion; revived in modern Paganism.

offr.name: Offerings
offr.desc: Food, drink, incense or goods given to gods, spirits or ancestors.
offr.note: Nearly universal from the Neolithic onward.

sacr.name: Animal sacrifice
sacr.note: Ancient Near East, Vedic yajña, Greek and Roman religion; still practised in Islam (Eid al-Adha), by Samaritans, and in African and Afro-diasporic religions.

hsac.name: Human sacrifice (historical)
hsac.note: Attested in Shang China, among the Aztec and Inca, in Hawaiʻi, in Kerma (Nubia) retainer burials, and elsewhere. Some claims, such as Carthaginian child sacrifice, remain debated.

fire.name: Sacred fire
fire.desc: Fire is a holy element, a divine presence or the vehicle of offerings.
fire.note: Proto-Indo-Iranian: Vedic Agni and the Zoroastrian fire temple; also Baltic and Roman (Vesta).

pray.name: Personal prayer
pray.desc: Individuals speak directly to the divine.

fpry.name: Fixed daily prayer times
fpry.desc: Set prayers at prescribed hours (Zoroastrian gāhs, Jewish services, Islamic salat, Christian hours).
fpry.note: Zoroastrian five gāhs are probably the earliest; Judaism, Islam, monastic Christianity and the Bahá'í Faith followed.

medi.name: Meditation and contemplation
medi.desc: Training the mind through stillness, concentration or contemplation.
medi.note: Śramaṇa and Upanishadic India (c. 6th c. BCE); separately in Daoism, Neoplatonism, Christian hesychasm and Sufi dhikr.

devo.name: Loving devotion to a personal god
devo.desc: Emotional surrender and love toward a deity (bhakti).
devo.note: Tamil bhakti saints (6th–9th c.), Sufism, Pure Land and Christian devotion.

sham.name: Shamanic trance
sham.desc: A specialist journeys in trance to the spirit world to heal or guide.
sham.note: Inferred for the Upper Paleolithic; the word comes from Evenki (Siberia).

poss.name: Spirit possession or mediumship
poss.desc: Gods or spirits speak through a human medium.
poss.note: West African and Afro-diasporic religions, Korean mudang, Chinese tangki, Spiritualism and Spiritism.

ente.name: Sacred plants or drinks
ente.desc: Mind-altering substances used as sacraments (soma, peyote, ayahuasca, cannabis, wine).
ente.note: Vedic soma and Avestan haoma; Chavín San Pedro cactus (c. 900 BCE); the Native American Church and Santo Daime.

danc.name: Ecstatic music and dance
danc.desc: Drumming, dance or song brings people into communion with the divine.
danc.note: San trance dance, Sufi samā', Pentecostal worship, Hasidic dancing, Vodou and Candomblé.

heal.name: Spiritual healing
heal.desc: Healing through spiritual means is central.
heal.note: Shamanic healing, African diviner-healers, Pentecostal and Christian Science healing, Tenrikyō.

divn.name: Divination and oracles
divn.desc: Reading the will of gods or fate through signs, lots, oracles or omens.
divn.note: Shang oracle bones, Mesopotamian liver omens, Delphi, Yoruba Ifá, the Yijing.

fest.name: Seasonal festivals
fest.desc: A calendar of feasts tied to seasons, harvests and solstices.
fest.note: Neolithic and megalithic monuments aligned to solstices (Newgrange, Stonehenge).

sabb.name: Weekly or regular holy day
sabb.desc: A recurring sacred rest or gathering day (Sabbath, Sunday, Jumu'ah, uposatha).
sabb.note: The Israelite Sabbath; parallels in the Buddhist uposatha.

pilg.name: Pilgrimage
pilg.note: Prehistoric gathering sites; later Delphi, Jerusalem, Mecca, Varanasi, Bodh Gaya, Santiago.

tmpl.name: Temples and shrines
tmpl.note: Göbekli Tepe (c. 9600 BCE) is among the earliest monumental ritual sites.

icon.name: Sacred images
icon.desc: Statues, icons or images of the divine are venerated.
icon.note: Upper Paleolithic figurines; temple statues in Sumer and Egypt; Hindu mūrti, Christian icons, Buddha images.

anic.name: Ban on images of God
anic.desc: The divine must not be depicted (aniconism).
anic.note: Israelite religion, then Judaism and Islam; also Reformed Protestantism, Sikhism, and the Arabian and Nabataean stone cults.

init.name: Initiation rites
init.desc: Rituals of entry or coming of age (baptism, upanayana, amrit, bar mitzvah).
init.note: Probably Paleolithic; universal in some form.

wash.name: Ritual washing or baptism
wash.note: Egypt, Indus (the Great Bath?), Jewish mikveh, Christian baptism, Islamic wuḍū', Shinto misogi, Mandaean masbuta.

meal.name: Sacred meal
meal.desc: A shared meal with sacred meaning (Eucharist, langar, Passover, Mithraic banquet).
meal.note: Neolithic feasting at Göbekli Tepe; Mithraic and Christian sacred meals.

myst.name: Mystery initiation
myst.desc: Secret rites reveal hidden truths to initiates.
myst.note: Eleusis (attested from c. 600 BCE), Mithraism, Isis, Tantra, Freemasonry, Wicca.

monk.name: Monasticism
monk.desc: Communities of monks or nuns living apart under a rule.
monk.note: Jain and Buddhist sanghas (5th c. BCE) are the earliest; Christian monasticism follows in 3rd–4th c. Egypt.

asce.name: Asceticism
asce.desc: Self-denial and austerity for spiritual ends.
asce.note: Śramaṇa India, Pythagoreans, Christian desert fathers, Sufis.

fast.name: Ritual fasting
fast.desc: Prescribed fasts (Yom Kippur, Lent, Ramadan, ekādaśī, Jain upavāsa).
fast.note: Widespread in the ancient Near East, India and the Americas.

diet.name: Dietary laws
diet.desc: Forbidden and permitted foods (kashrut, halal, Ital, Jain diet).
diet.note: Israelite and Zoroastrian purity laws; Hindu, Jain, Islamic and Adventist codes.

vegt.name: Vegetarianism
vegt.desc: Meat is avoided for religious reasons.
vegt.note: Jain, Buddhist and Hindu ahiṃsā; Orphics and Pythagoreans; Manichaean elect, Cathars, Adventists.

alco.name: Alcohol prohibited
alco.note: The Buddhist fifth precept, Islam, Bahá'í, Sikh Khalsa, Latter-day Saints, Methodist temperance.

dres.name: Religious dress or hair rules
dres.desc: Required head-coverings, garments or hair (kippah, hijab, turban, dreadlocks).
dres.note: Widespread; formalized in Judaism, Islam, Sikhism, Amish and Rastafari.

circ.name: Circumcision
circ.note: Depicted in Egypt c. 2300 BCE; covenant sign in Israelite religion; customary in Islam and Ethiopian Christianity.

celi.name: Celibate clergy or elite
celi.desc: Priests, monks or an elect class must be celibate.
celi.note: Buddhist and Jain monastics, Manichaean elect, Latin Catholic priests (mandatory from 1139), Cathar perfecti, Shakers.

rlaw.name: Comprehensive religious law
rlaw.desc: A detailed legal system covering all of life (halakha, sharia, dharmaśāstra, canon law).
rlaw.note: Israelite and rabbinic Judaism, Islam, Hindu dharmaśāstra, Zoroastrian Vendidad, Catholic canon law.

tith.name: Tithing
tith.desc: A fixed share of income is given to the religion.
tith.note: Ancient Near East and Israelite tithe; Christian churches; Latter-day Saints (10%).

oral.name: Oral transmission
oral.desc: Sacred knowledge is passed down mainly by memory, song and story rather than a written canon.
oral.note: The original form of all religion; still primary in many Indigenous traditions.

scri.name: Sacred scripture
scri.desc: A body of written sacred texts or a canon.
scri.note: Sumerian temple hymns (c. 2500 BCE) and Egyptian Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE) are the earliest religious writing.

revl.name: New or ongoing revelation
revl.desc: God continues to reveal truth through new prophets or living inspiration.
revl.note: Montanists, Manichaeans, Islam, the Latter-day Saints, Bahá'í, Quakers' inner light, Tenrikyō.

gnos.name: Esoteric knowledge (gnosis)
gnos.desc: Salvation or truth comes through hidden, inner knowledge.
gnos.note: Gnosticism, Hermeticism, Kabbalah, Ismaili bāṭin, Tantra, Theosophy.

foun.name: Founder or prophet
foun.desc: The tradition traces itself to a specific founder or prophet.
foun.note: Zoroaster, Mahāvīra and the Buddha are among the earliest; Jesus, Muhammad, Nanak and many modern founders follow.

guru.name: Teacher lineages
guru.desc: Authority passes through living masters (guru, shaykh, rebbe, roshi).
guru.note: Upanishadic teacher–student lineages; Sufi silsilas, Zen transmission, Hasidic dynasties.

prie.name: Priesthood
prie.desc: A priestly class, often hereditary, performs the rites for others.
prie.note: From the first temple cities (Sumer, Egypt) and Vedic brahmins to Catholic and Orthodox priests and Zoroastrian mobeds.

hier.name: Central hierarchy
hier.desc: Organized ranks under a central head (pope, patriarch, Dalai Lama, Universal House of Justice).
hier.note: Roman Catholic papacy, Tibetan Buddhism, Latter-day Saints, Twelver marja'iyya.

cong.name: Lay-led congregations
cong.desc: Local communities run themselves, often without priests.
cong.note: Synagogues after 70 CE, Protestant congregationalism, Quakers, Sikh sangat, Bahá'í.

ethn.name: Ethnic or hereditary membership
ethn.desc: Belonging comes mainly by birth into a people or caste.
ethn.note: Most ancient and Indigenous religions; Judaism, Druze, Yazidis, Parsis, Mandaeans.

univ.name: Universal and open to all
univ.desc: Anyone of any people can join.
univ.note: Buddhism (5th c. BCE) is the earliest universal missionary religion; mystery cults, Christianity and Islam followed.

miss.name: Missionary outreach
miss.note: Ashokan Buddhism (3rd c. BCE), Manichaeism, Christianity, Islam, Latter-day Saints.

sync.name: Openly blends traditions
sync.note: Hellenistic religions, Manichaeism, Afro-Atlantic religions, Caodaism, Theosophy, the New Age.

trads.d: Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh in Israel, roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago, some with red ochre and ochre-painted shells, are among the earliest hints of ritual care for the dead. Neanderthals also buried their dead. Whether this implies belief in an afterlife is debated.
trads.an: Qafzeh burials dated c. 92,000 years ago (thermoluminescence) with ochre and ochre-painted shells; wording adjusted to 'roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago'.

trads.d: Cave paintings in Sulawesi (over 45,000 years old) and Europe (Chauvet, Lascaux), the Lion-man figurine and richly furnished graves suggest a world of animal spirits, ritual specialists and initiation. Details are inferred by comparison with recent hunter-gatherers.
trads.an: Lion-man figurine c. 38,000 BCE; shamanism inferred for the Upper Paleolithic; meaning of 'Venus' figurines debated.

trads.n: Göbekli Tepe and early Neolithic cult sites
trads.d: Massive carved T-shaped pillars at Göbekli Tepe (from about 9600 BCE) are among the oldest monumental ritual structures. They were built by people on the threshold of farming and were probably used for feasting gatherings.
trads.an: Earliest dates c. 9500 calBC; start changed from 9600 to 9500 BCE.

trads.d: Early farmers at Jericho and Çatalhöyük buried ancestors under house floors, plastered and painted skulls, and made female and animal figurines. These practices tied fertility, the household and the farming year together.
trads.an: Çatalhöyük c. 7500–5700 BCE; Neolithic burials inside houses and plastered skulls in the Levant.

trads.d: Builders of passage tombs, stone circles and alignments (Carnac, Newgrange around 3200 BCE, Stonehenge around 3000–2000 BCE) gathered the dead in communal tombs and aligned monuments to the solstices.
trads.an: Newgrange 3200–3100 BCE; Stonehenge initial form 3100 BCE, final c. 2600 BCE, use ended c. 1600 BCE; solstice alignment.

trads.d: Reconstructed from shared words and myths in its daughter traditions: a sky father (*Dyḗws Ph₂tḗr), a thunder god (*Perkʷunos), a dawn goddess (*H₂éwsōs) and a principle of fitting order (*h₂értus) that reappears as Vedic ṛta and Avestan arəta/aša.
trads.an: Sky Father (*Dyḗws Ph₂tḗr), thunder god (*Perkʷunos), dawn goddess (*H₂éwsōs) and order (*h₂értus → ṛta, arəta) confirmed; archaic PIE dated c. 4500–4000 BCE so start moved to 4500 BCE; horse-sacrifice and guest–host claims removed from the description as not confirmed in the checked source.

trads.d: Shared ancestor of Vedic and Iranian religion, tied to the Sintashta culture: a sacred pressed drink (*sauma, later soma or haoma), hymn-singing priests, two classes of gods (*daywás and *Hasuras), Mitra, and a cosmic truth-order (*Hrta, later ṛta and aša). A fire god (*Hagníš) is reconstructed.
trads.an: The Proto-Indo-Iranian period is tied to the Sintashta culture (c. 2050–1900 BCE), so dates were changed to 2100–1700 BCE. Sacred drink *sauma (soma/haoma, probably ephedra), priests, *daywás and *Hasuras, *Hrta (ṛta/aša) and Mitra confirmed. A fire god (*Hagníš) is reconstructed but no specific fire ritual, so the description was reworded.

trads.d: The script is undeciphered. Seals, the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro and figurines hint at ritual bathing, fertility imagery and a seated horned figure some link to the later Shiva. All such links are speculative.
trads.an: Mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE; undeciphered script; Great Bath possibly ritual; female figurines and the 'Pashupati seal' interpretations are debated or speculative.

trads.d: The Yangshao, Longshan and Liangzhu cultures left jade ritual objects (the cong and bi), ancestor burials and early bone divination, forerunners of Shang religion.
trads.an: Liangzhu (3300–2300 BCE) ritual jade cong and bi, elite burials and the Yaoshan altar confirmed. Bone divination in this period is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Clay dogū figures, stone circles and burials from Japan's long Jōmon period suggest animist and fertility beliefs that may underlie later kami worship.
trads.an: Jōmon c. 14,000–300 BCE; ornate dogū figurines; burial mounds and grave goods; elements described as precursors of Shinto. Animist and fertility beliefs are inferred and not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: The first peoples of the Americas carried Upper Paleolithic hunter traditions, likely animist and shamanic, across Beringia.
trads.an: The Anzick-1 child burial in Montana (c. 12,900 BP) was covered in red ochre with over 100 Clovis tools, a deliberate ritual burial. Its genome links Clovis people to living Native Americans and supports the Beringia migration. 'Animist and shamanic' is an inference from later ethnography, not directly attested.

trads.d: Reconstructed beliefs in spirits of the dead (*qanitu) and ancestors. The Austronesian expansion carried them from Taiwan across the Pacific and Indian oceans.
trads.an: The 'Out of Taiwan' expansion ran c. 3000–1500 BCE; animism and ancestor effigies confirmed. The reconstructed *qanitu and taboo terms are not covered by the checked portion of the source.

trads.d: Reconstructed shared Semitic religion. Only a generic word for god, *ʔil-, can be reconstructed with confidence; it later became the proper name El. It is ancestral to Akkadian, Canaanite and Arabian religion.
trads.an: Only a generic word for deity, *ʔil-, is reconstructed (later El as a proper name); named sun, moon and storm gods are not confirmed. Proto-Semitic is dated c. 4500–3900 BCE with a disputed homeland, so start moved from 3500 to 4000 BCE and the description was reworded.

trads.d: City gods such as An, Enlil, Enki and Inanna lived in temples tended by priests, and humans were created to serve them. The dead went to a dreary underworld. Sumer produced the earliest flood story and the first named author, the priestess Enheduanna (around 2300 BCE).
trads.an: Gods tended in temples by priests; humans created to serve the gods; dim underworld (Irkalla); Gilgamesh holds the earliest flood reference.

trads.d: Akkadian-speaking heirs of Sumer. Marduk, made supreme in Babylon from Hammurabi's time, defeats Tiamat and shapes heaven and earth in the Enuma Elish. The Epic of Gilgamesh retold the flood, and omens were read from entrails and stars. Temples were revived in the Parthian period, and the religion had almost died out by 400–500 CE.
trads.an: Mesopotamian religion 'had almost completely died out by approximately 400–500 AD', with temples revived in Assyrian vassal states in the Parthian period; end moved from 300 to 400 CE. Marduk made supreme under Hammurabi (18th c. BCE); description reworded.

trads.d: Harran kept an old Semitic star and planet worship long after the rest of Mesopotamian religion had faded. Facing al-Ma'mun's ultimatum in 830, its people took the protected name 'Sabians'. Medieval writers say they honored Hermes Trismegistus, but scholars find no firm evidence for a Hermetic or Neoplatonic identity.
trads.an: Harranian polytheism with planetary cults survived into the Islamic era; in 830 al-Ma'mun's ultimatum led them to adopt the name Sabians. Hermetic/Neoplatonic identity attested by medieval sources but with 'no firm evidence'; end date uncertain (11th c.). Description softened.

trads.d: Burials with grave goods at Badari and Naqada, figurines placed near the dead, and early royal symbolism (the Gebel el-Arak knife) foreshadow pharaonic religion.
trads.an: Naqada I–III c. 3900–2900 BCE; figurines near bodies suggest mortuary ritual; Naqada III grave goods elaborate; first pharaohs and royal motifs (Gebel el-Arak knife). Animal burials are not covered by the checked source, so they were removed from the description.

trads.d: Gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis and Horus upheld Ma'at, the eternal order of the universe, and the pharaoh was identified with Horus. The dead were judged by weighing the heart (fully developed by the New Kingdom), and the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom are among the oldest religious writings. Philae, the last temple, closed around 537 CE.
trads.an: Pharaoh identified with Horus, Ma'at, ka/ba confirmed; Philae closure dated AD 537 (Procopius), though Dijkstra argues organized cult ended in the 5th c.; end moved from 550 to 537.

trads.d: Pharaoh Akhenaten promoted the sun disk Aten as the sole god, closing other cults. It is often called the first recorded monotheism, though some scholars prefer monolatry. It was erased after his death.
trads.an: Akhenaten replaced Amun with the Aten; monotheism vs. monolatry/henotheism is disputed; reign began 1353 or 1351 BCE.

trads.d: Modern revivals of Egyptian religion, such as Kemetic Orthodoxy (founded 1988), reconstruct temple rites and devotion to the netjeru (gods).
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Tamara Siuda (born 1969) founded Kemetic Orthodoxy.

trads.d: Texts from Ugarit describe El as father of the gods, Baal as storm god, the goddesses Asherah and Anat, and Mot (Death). This religion is the direct background of early Israelite religion.
trads.an: El heads the pantheon with Asherah; Baal (Hadad) storm god, Anat, Mot; Ugaritic texts c. 1275 BCE, Ugarit destroyed c. 1200 BCE.

trads.d: Melqart, Tanit and Baal Hammon spread with Phoenician traders. Scholars still debate whether the tophet burials of infants at Carthage are evidence of child sacrifice.
trads.an: Melqart, Tanit and Baal Hammon confirmed; child sacrifice at Carthage remains debated.

trads.d: Early worship of Yahweh grew out of Canaanite religion, possibly at first alongside other deities such as Asherah, though scholars debate this. Prophets and reformers, among them King Josiah in 622 BCE, pushed toward exclusive worship of Yahweh, a ban on images and covenant law. Biblical tradition places Moses earlier; this entry follows the academic reconstruction.
trads.an: Whether Asherah was worshipped as Yahweh's consort is debated (some read ʾašērāh as 'holy place'); description now says 'possibly'.
kt: Early strata of the Hebrew Bible
Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions

trads.d: Tribal gods such as Hubal and the goddesses al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt were honored at sacred stones and shrines, and the Kaaba in Mecca was already a pilgrimage site. Jinn haunted the desert. Some Arabs were Jews, Christians or ḥanīf monotheists.
trads.an: Hubal, al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt; sacred stones; Kaaba as pre-Islamic pilgrimage site; jinn; Jewish, Christian and ḥanīf communities.

trads.d: Dushara was the Nabataean patron god. He and other deities were honored as god-stones, often carved into the rock faces of Petra and sometimes given simple features.
trads.an: Dushara was the Nabataean patron god; god-stones were often carved in rock faces and could bear incised features, so 'plain aniconic stones' was overstated. Reworded.

trads.d: Gods of the pre-Hittite people of Anatolia, such as the Sun Goddess of Arinna, were later absorbed by the Hittites.
trads.an: Sun goddess of Arinna and Telipinu are Hattic deities absorbed by the Hittites.

trads.d: The storm god Teshub and the Kumarbi succession myth, a likely ancestor of Hesiod's Theogony, passed to the Hittites and the Greeks.
trads.an: Teshub; Song of Kumarbi resembles Cronus in Hesiod's Theogony.
kt: Kumarbi Cycle (Song of Kumarbi, Song of Ullikummi)

trads.d: Called the 'land of a thousand gods', the Hittites added Hattian, Hurrian and Mesopotamian deities to an Indo-European core and kept detailed ritual tablets.
trads.an: Hittite empire c. 1600–1180 BCE; 'thousand gods'; Hattian Sun goddess of Arinna; Hurrian Teshub and the Kumarbi cycle paralleling Hesiod; Mesopotamian deities adopted.

trads.d: Gods such as Inshushinak and Pinikir were worshipped at ziggurats such as Chogha Zanbil.
trads.an: Inshushinak (Susa's protector, later head of the supreme triad), Pinikir, Humban and Napirisha; prominent mother goddesses (Kiririsha); Chogha Zanbil as religious capital; civilization c. 3200–539 BCE.

trads.d: Kerma's royal burials included sacrificed retainers. Later Napatan and Meroitic kings worshipped Amun alongside the lion god Apedemak.
trads.an: Nubians adopted Amun worship. Apedemak not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Peak sanctuaries, the double axe, bull-leaping and goddess figures with snakes suggest a nature and goddess-centered religion. Without readable texts, most interpretation is uncertain.
trads.an: Peak sanctuaries, double axe, bull-leaping, snake-goddess figurines (possibly priestesses), and a dominant goddess. Cited sites run from c. 2900 to after 1400 BCE, with Mycenaean conquest c. 1450 BCE.

trads.d: Linear B tablets name gods later worshipped by the Greeks, including Poseidon (po-se-da-o) and Dionysus (di-wo-nu-so), as recipients of offerings. Some Minoan goddesses may lie behind Artemis and Athena.
trads.an: Date range c. 1600–1100 BCE confirmed. Linear B names Poseidon (po-se-da-o) and Dionysus (di-wo-nu-so); Hera only via an epithet in the checked source, so the description no longer lists Zeus and Hera as named.

trads.d: The Olympian gods, hero cults and civic festivals; oracles at Delphi; Panhellenic games; and the dead in Hades. There was no scripture or creed. Public sacrifice was banned by the Theodosian decrees (391–392).
trads.an: No revealed scripture; Delphi oracle; official persecution under Theodosius I from 381 culminating in the 391–392 decrees.
kt: Hesiod, Theogony and Works and Days

trads.d: Secret yearly rites of Demeter and Persephone, first attested in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (c. 650 BCE), promised initiates a better fate after death. From about 300 BCE men, women and slaves could be initiated if they spoke Greek and were free of blood guilt. Theodosius I closed them in 392.
trads.an: Earliest textual source is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (c. 650 BCE), so start moved from 600 to 650 BCE; afterlife reward confirmed; men, women and slaves initiated after c. 300 BCE (Greek speakers without blood guilt); closed by Theodosius I in 392, shrines looted by Alaric in 396.

trads.d: Ecstatic wine and dance rites of Dionysus. Gold tablets placed in initiates' graves give directions for the afterlife.
trads.an: Ecstatic wine, music and dance rites open to slaves, women and outsiders; Bacchic gold tablets direct the dead to the Lake of Memory. Attested 5th c. BCE–3rd c. CE, so dates moved from 600 BCE–400 CE to 500 BCE–300 CE.

trads.d: Orphics taught that the soul is divine and trapped in the body, reborn until purified. This is an early Western idea of reincarnation, joined with vegetarian rules and sacred poems attributed to Orpheus.
trads.an: Soul held in bondage by the Titanic body and reincarnated until initiation, poems attributed to Orpheus, 6th–5th c. BCE origins confirmed. Orphic vegetarianism is not covered by the checked source (it is attested in Plato, Laws 782c).

trads.d: Pythagoras's communities held property in common, kept secret teachings, ate no meat and taught the transmigration of souls and the sacredness of number.
trads.an: Pythagoras taught reincarnation.

trads.d: Stoics held that the cosmos is a single divine rational fire (Logos). Virtue lay in living according to nature, all people were citizens of one world, and the cosmos was destroyed and renewed in endless cycles.
trads.an: Stoic God linked to the logos.

trads.d: Epicurus taught that gods exist but do not interfere, that the soul dissolves at death, and that freedom from fear is the good life.
trads.an: Founded 307 BCE; gods exist but do not intervene; the soul is mortal; ataraxia as the goal; declined by the late 3rd c. CE.

trads.d: Plotinus taught that all reality emanates from the One and the soul can return to it through contemplation. Later Neoplatonists added theurgy, ritual that draws on divine power. It deeply shaped Christian, Jewish and Islamic mysticism.
trads.an: Ammonius Saccas and Plotinus (c. 205–271), who taught in Rome from c. 245; the One and emanation; Iamblichus's theurgy; Academy closed 529; influence on Christian, Jewish and Islamic thought.

trads.d: Phrygia's mountain mother goddess, named as Matar Kubileya in a 6th-century-BCE inscription, came to Rome in 204 BCE on the advice of the Sibylline oracle. Her eunuch galli priests castrated themselves in devotion to Attis.
trads.an: Phrygian 'Matar Kubileya' inscription dates to the 6th c. BCE, so start moved from 800 to 600 BCE; arrival in Rome 204 BCE and eunuch galli confirmed.

trads.d: Isis worship, reshaped for Greeks and Romans, offered initiates personal salvation. Her temple at Philae was among the last pagan temples to close.
trads.an: Isis among Rome's international deities; her mysteries were banned under Augustus and Tiberius, then later flourished.

trads.d: Etruscan religion was famous for its books of ritual and for reading the will of the gods from livers and lightning. Rome inherited both.
trads.an: Haruspicy of Etruscan origin used in Roman public cult; Etruscan religion strongly shaped augury.

trads.d: Roman religion was a civic contract with the gods (pax deorum) kept through state priesthoods, the Vestal fire and augury, and later the imperial cult. It absorbed gods from every conquered people. The start date is Rome's traditional founding year.
trads.an: Pax deorum; Vestal fire (extinguished by Theodosius I); augury; Etruscan haruspicy; imperial cult; foreign cults absorbed. Christianity official from 380.
kt: Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods

trads.d: A secret, men-only cult of Mithras slaying a bull. Members met in cave-like temples, rose through seven grades and shared ritual meals. Its link to the Iranian Mithra is debated.
trads.an: Popular in the Roman army from the 1st to 4th c. CE; origins disputed (1st c. BCE or CE); largely men only; seven grades; sacred banquets; underground mithraea; Iranian link debated.

trads.d: Druid priests oversaw sacrifice and divination, and Caesar reported that they taught the soul passes into new bodies. Roman reports of human sacrifice may be exaggerated, though rare finds support some. Medieval Irish sources record four seasonal festivals, Samhain, Imbolc, Beltaine and Lughnasadh, but which festivals the ancient Celts kept is uncertain.
trads.an: Roman reports of human sacrifice (possibly exaggerated) plus rare archaeological evidence; gradual conversion from the 5th c. Medieval Irish sources record Beltaine, Lughnasadh, Samhain and Imbolc, but it is unclear which festivals the ancient Celts held, so the description is softened. Caesar's report of transmigration is not covered by the checked source.
kt: Later Irish and Welsh texts: Lebor Gabála Érenn

trads.d: Druid orders revived in the 18th century (the Ancient Order of Druids, 1781), and modern groups such as OBOD (1964) center nature, poetry and the solstices.
trads.an: Ancient Order of Druids founded 1781; Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids founded 1964 by Ross Nichols.

trads.d: Tacitus described sacred groves, divination by lots, and gods such as Wodan and Thor (Donar). Bog finds include possible sacrificial victims.
trads.an: Tacitus (reliability questioned) describes sacred groves and lot divination; gods Wodanaz, Thunraz, Tiwaz, Frijjō; deposits including human remains in bogs and springs; weekday names.

trads.d: Odin, Thor and Freyja; the world tree Yggdrasil; Valhalla for the slain; seiðr magic; and Ragnarök at the world's end. Iceland adopted Christianity at the Althing in 999 or 1000, and Sweden was fully Christian by the early 12th century.
trads.an: Iceland adopted Christianity at the Althing in 999 (often given as 1000); Sweden fully Christian by the early 12th c.; Yggdrasil, Valhalla, Ragnarök and seiðr confirmed.

trads.d: The gods Woden, Thunor and Tiw gave English its weekday names. England converted from 597 onward.
trads.an: Bede (c. 731) is the main source on Anglo-Saxon paganism; the 597 mission date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Modern revival of Germanic and Norse religion. Iceland recognized the Ásatrúarfélagið in 1973. Most groups are open to all, though some 'folkish' groups are not.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson (1924–1993) founded Ásatrú in Iceland.

trads.d: Perun the thunderer, Veles of the underworld, and many-headed idols such as Svantevit at Arkona, which was destroyed in 1168.
trads.an: Perun and Veles; Svetovid's temple at Arkona destroyed in 1168 by Valdemar I; Christianization between the 8th and 13th c.

trads.d: Modern Slavic native faith movements, organized from the early 20th century and expanding after the Soviet collapse. They range from nature-centered to nationalist.
trads.an: The checked source dates the organized revival to the early 20th century, so start moved from 1980 to 1930.
kt: Book of Veles (forgery, used by some)

trads.d: Sacred groves and an eternal fire for the thunder god Perkūnas. Lithuania was Europe's last officially pagan state, baptized in 1387.
trads.an: Dievas the sky god and Saule confirmed; the checked source places Baltic Christianization from the 15th c. Lithuania's 1387 baptism is the standard date but was not covered by this source.

trads.d: Baltic revivals: Latvian Dievturība (1925) and Lithuanian Romuva (1967), with folk song and fire rites.
trads.an: Romuva and Dievturība listed; founding years from standard references.

trads.d: Reconstructed worship of the Olympian gods. Organized groups formed in Greece in the 1990s, and the state recognized Hellenism as a 'known religion' in 2017. Practitioners differ on animal sacrifice; many offer food or libations instead.
trads.an: Organized revival in Greece from the 1990s and recognized as a 'known religion' in 2017 confirmed; adherents are divided on animal sacrifice, and the description now says so.

trads.d: Worship of Mithra, Anahita and other gods with haoma and fire rituals, before and alongside Zoroaster's reform.
trads.an: Mithra (covenants), Anahita (waters), the daivas, haoma pressed in the yasna, and sacred fire. Worship took place in the open without images or temples, and the religion was gradually displaced by Zoroastrianism.

trads.d: Zoroaster taught that the wise lord Ahura Mazda opposes the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu, and that humans choose sides through 'good thoughts, good words, good deeds'. Its judgment, heaven and hell, resurrection and coming savior shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Zoroaster's date is disputed, with estimates from about 1500 to 500 BCE.
trads.an: Britannica: Zarathustra 'flourished before the 6th century BCE'; dates remain disputed (estimates c. 1500–500 BCE). Bridge of the Requiter (Chinvat), heaven/hell, resurrection, savior (Saoshyant), fire cult and influence on Judaism, Christianity and Islam all confirmed.

trads.d: A Sasanian-era current that made Zurvan (Time) the father of both Ahura Mazda (Ohrmazd) and Angra Mainyu (Ahriman).
trads.an: Britannica: Zurvan (Time) as father of Ohrmazd and Ahriman; wording changed from 'above both' to 'father of both'.

trads.d: Mazdak, prominent under King Kavad I (r. 498–531), preached sharing of goods, opposition to war and abstention from meat. He was executed under Khusrau I.
trads.an: Prominent under Kavad I (r. 498–531); communal ownership, opposed war and meat-eating. Killed by Khusrau I; the 'massacre in 528' detail was replaced with 'executed under Khusrau I'.

trads.d: Mani (born 216) claimed to complete the teachings of Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus. He taught that particles of light are trapped in dark matter and freed by the Elect, who ate no meat and drank no wine. The faith spread from Roman Iberia to China. The Ming banned it in 1370, though a remnant survives at the Cao'an temple in Fujian.
trads.an: Mani born 216 near Ctesiphon; saw himself as completing Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus; the Elect abstained from meat and wine. In China it was banned by the Ming in 1370 and absorbed into Buddhism and Daoism by the end of the 14th c., with a remnant at the Cao'an temple. End moved from 1600 to 1400.

trads.d: Zoroastrians who left Iran for India after the Islamic conquest. Britannica dates the emigration to the 10th century onward; the community's Qissa-i Sanjan suggests an earlier arrival. They generally accept members only by birth.
trads.an: Britannica dates Parsi emigration to India 'from the 10th century onward'; start moved from 800 to 900 CE and the description notes the traditional earlier date (Qissa-i Sanjan).

trads.r: Northern Iraq, Syria, Turkey, Armenia, diaspora
trads.d: Yazidis revere one God and seven holy beings led by Tawûsê Melek, the Peacock Angel, and trace their reformer to the Sufi Sheikh Adi (died 1162). They practise pilgrimage to Lalish and accept members only by birth. Elements may be much older.
trads.an: Sheikh Adi died 1162; seven angels led by Tawûsî Melek; rebirth ('changing of the shirt'); Lalish pilgrimage; strict endogamy.
kt: Meshaf Reş and Kitêba Cilwe (late compilations)

trads.d: A Kurdish faith founded by Sultan Sahak in the late 14th century. It teaches successive divine manifestations and rebirth. Its scripture is the Kalâm-e Saranjâm, and it has roughly 0.5–1 million followers in Iran and more in Iraq.
trads.an: Sultan Sahak dated to the late 14th c., so start moved from 1350 to 1380; successive divine manifestations and transmigration; Kalâm-e Saranjâm from the 15th c.; c. 0.5–1 million in Iran plus 75,000–250,000 in Iraq.

trads.d: The word 'shaman' comes from the Evenki language. The shaman drums and journeys through a layered cosmos joined by a world tree to heal and guide souls.
trads.an: 'Shaman' comes from Evenki; shamans journey to celestial and underground realms to rescue souls and heal; 123,423 people in Russia's 2002 census belonged to groups mainly following traditional beliefs. The world tree is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: The noaidi (shaman) used a drum. People made offerings at sacred stones (sieidi). It was suppressed in the 17th–18th centuries and revived today.
trads.an: The noaidi mediated with the underworld using a drum; sieidi sacred stones; reindeer offerings; practised until the 18th c. The modern revival is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Ukko the sky god, Tuonela the land of the dead and the sung lore preserved in the Kalevala. A modern revival (Suomenusko) began in 2002.
trads.an: Ukko, Tuonela and oral runo songs (written down as the Kalevala by Lönnrot) confirmed. Forbidden from the 1600s, but sacred groves were used in the 1700s, beliefs mixed with Christianity into the 19th c. and folk magic lasted to the early 20th c. End moved from 1700 to 1850.

trads.d: The Mari people's traditional religion has continued alongside Orthodox Christianity for centuries. Priests (karts) lead prayers and animal offerings in sacred groves, and about 15% of Mari El's population identified with it in a 2004 survey.
trads.an: Mari native religion has existed continuously alongside Orthodoxy, with about 15% of Mari El's population identifying with it (2004 survey). The 'Europe's last pagan religion' tagline was removed because the checked source does not use it.

trads.d: Worship of Tengri, the Eternal Blue Sky, first appears in Chinese chronicles in the 4th century BCE as the Xiongnu sky god and was later held by Turks and Mongols. Umay is a goddess of children. It has been revived since the 1990s in Mongolia, Central Asia and Siberia.
trads.an: Tengri first appears in Chinese chronicles in the 4th c. BCE as the Xiongnu sky god, so start moved from 300 to 350 BCE; Umay; revival since the 1990s.

trads.d: A 1904 prophetic movement among the Altai that rejected blood sacrifice and shamans' drums and awaited a savior, Oirot Khan.
trads.an: Altaian Burkhanism (1904).

trads.d: All things have kamuy (spirits). In the iyomante ceremony a raised bear was sent back to the gods.
trads.an: Kamuy in all of nature; iyomante bear-sending (banned 1955, revived as an annual festival); inau offerings; settlements of the 13th–17th c.

trads.d: Rites for the Yarlung divine kings, royal tombs and divination, before Buddhism became the state religion.
trads.an: Ancient bon priests appeased spirits, guided the dead, sacrificed animals and buried the dead with jewels; a court religion legitimized the Yarlung kings with sacrificial, oracular and shamanic rites (dated by Thurman to c. 100 BCE under Pudegungyal). Start moved from 500 BCE to 100 BCE.

trads.d: Bön was organized as a monastic religion in the 11th century and traces itself to the teacher Tönpa Shenrab. It parallels Tibetan Buddhism closely while claiming older roots.
trads.an: Yungdrung Bön emerged in the 10th–11th c. with Shenchen Luga's early-11th-c. treasure discoveries; Menri Monastery founded 1405; c. 400,000 followers on the Tibetan Plateau (2019). Scholars debate how much is pre-Buddhist.

trads.d: After the exile, the rebuilt Temple, the Torah canon and strict monotheism became central. Ideas of angels, Satan, resurrection, final judgment and a messiah developed, partly in contact with Persian thought.
trads.an: c. 516 BCE–70 CE; Persian and Babylonian apocalyptic influence (Daniel 7–12); messianic hopes; Pharisees gave rise to Rabbinic Judaism.

trads.r: Mount Gerizim (West Bank) and Holon, Israel
trads.d: Samaritans hold only their own Pentateuch as scripture and Mount Gerizim as the holy place, and still sacrifice lambs there at Passover. The split from Judeans was gradual; scholars often place the decisive break in the Hasmonean period. About 900 remain (2024).
trads.an: About 900 people (2024); Passover lamb sacrifice on Mount Gerizim continues; Samaritan Pentateuch only. The schism date is widely debated (a gradual process, with a decisive break often placed in the Hasmonean period), so start moved from 400 to 300 BCE at low confidence.

trads.d: The priestly Temple elite accepted only the written Torah and denied resurrection. They vanished with the Temple in 70 CE.
trads.an: Lost prominence with the Temple's fall in 70 CE but probably continued informally for decades; end moved from 70 to 100.

trads.d: Communal, purity-focused sectarians, probably including the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls, who expected a war between the Sons of Light and the Sons of Darkness.
trads.an: Essenes criticized the Temple, expected good's victory over evil, and some lived in isolation. Celibacy and Qumran are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: After the Temple fell, the Pharisaic sages rebuilt Judaism around Torah study, synagogue prayer and halakha (law), recorded in the Mishnah and Talmud. Hillel summed up the Torah as 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow'. About 15 million Jews today.
trads.an: Pharisees succeeded by the rabbis, giving rise to Rabbinic Judaism.

trads.d: Karaites reject the rabbinic Oral Law and read the Hebrew Bible directly. The movement took shape in the early 9th century, drawing on Anan ben David's 8th-century challenge.
trads.an: The checked source dates Karaism to the early 9th c., with Anan ben David's 8th-c. movement as forerunner; start moved from 760 to 800.

trads.d: Ethiopian Jews kept a pre-rabbinic, Torah-based faith (Haymanot) with their own monks and Ge'ez scriptures. Many historians date the community's formation to the 14th–16th centuries; others argue for far older Jewish roots, and the community traces its descent to the tribe of Dan. Most of its 173,500 members now live in Israel.
trads.an: Scholars disagree. One school (Kaplan, Shelemay, Tamrat) sees the community forming in the 14th–16th c.; another (Messing, Waldman) sees ancient Jewish roots; the community's own account traces descent to the tribe of Dan. Start moved from 600 to 1350 at low confidence, with both views in the description. About 173,500 worldwide, mostly in Israel after Operations Moses (1984) and Solomon (1991).

trads.d: Jewish mysticism of the ten sefirot emanating from the infinite Ein Sof. Key texts are the Bahir (around 1180) and the Zohar (around 1280).
trads.an: Sefer ha-Bahir from 12th–13th-c. Provence; Zohar late 13th c. (Moses de León); sefirot and Ein Sof; Luria in 16th-c. Safed; shattering of the vessels, tikkun, gilgul.

trads.d: Isaac Luria taught that the divine vessels shattered at creation, and that humans repair the world (tikkun) through commandments and prayer.
trads.an: Luria systematized shevirat ha-kelim, tikkun and gilgul in 16th-c. Safed.

trads.d: A mass movement around Sabbatai Zevi, who proclaimed himself messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam in September 1666. His Dönmeh followers kept a secret faith in Ottoman lands, and their descendants are still found in Turkey today.
trads.an: Sabbatai Zevi proclaimed himself messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam on 15 September 1666; Dönmeh descendants persisted into 21st-c. Turkey. End changed to 1950 (as an organized religion), with a note.

trads.d: Jacob Frank's antinomian Sabbatean sect, whose members eventually converted to Catholicism.
trads.an: Jacob Frank's 18th-c. Sabbatean movement in Eastern Europe; Frank converted to Catholicism.

trads.d: Founded by the Baal Shem Tov, Hasidism stressed joyful devotion, song and dance and the holy rebbe (tzaddik). Rebbes lead dynasties.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Baal Shem Tov (1698–1760).

trads.d: Orthodoxy took shape as a movement in opposition to Reform. The first separate Orthodox congregation formed in Frankfurt under S. R. Hirsch in 1851. It holds the Torah and halakha to be divinely given and binding, and ranges from Modern Orthodox to Haredi.
trads.an: Orthodoxy became a self-conscious movement in opposition to Reform; the first separate Orthodox congregation (S. R. Hirsch, Frankfurt) dates to 1851. Start moved from 1820 to 1840, at low confidence.

trads.d: Reform treats halakha as non-binding and stresses ethical monotheism, social justice and progressive revelation. Its first milestone was Israel Jacobson's temple at Seesen (1810), and it took shape as a movement from around 1820.
trads.an: The checked source says Reform began c. 1820. Israel Jacobson's Seesen temple (1810) is the conventional first milestone, so 1810 is kept and noted as an early milestone.

trads.d: Conservative Judaism holds halakha binding but evolving. The Jewish Theological Seminary was founded in 1886–87.
trads.an: The checked source says Conservative Judaism originated in 19th-c. Germany and was institutionalized in the US. The JTS founding date (1886) was not covered.

trads.d: Mordecai Kaplan saw Judaism as an evolving civilization and God as a natural power for good.
trads.an: A 1922 American split from Conservative Judaism led by Mordecai Kaplan.

trads.d: Founded by Rabbi Sherwin Wine, Humanistic Judaism celebrates Jewish culture and history without God.
trads.an: Founded in Detroit in 1963 by Rabbi Sherwin Wine; Society for Humanistic Judaism founded 1969.

trads.d: Followers of Jesus of Nazareth proclaimed him the Messiah, risen from the dead. He taught love of enemies and that God's kingdom was coming. The movement practised baptism and a shared meal.
trads.an: Early Christianity emerged as a Jewish sect.

trads.d: Torah-observant followers of Jesus, many of whom saw him as a human prophet and messiah rather than divine. They faded by the 5th century.
trads.an: Jewish Christianity discussed.

trads.d: Paul's mission opened the faith to gentiles without circumcision or Jewish law. Bishops, the New Testament canon, martyr cults and creeds took shape.
trads.an: Paul's mission to the Gentiles; the Council of Jerusalem (c. 48–50) freed Gentile converts from circumcision; bishops at Rome, Antioch and elsewhere; Paul's letters are the earliest writings and the gospels date to c. 70–100; martyrs from Nero onward; the period ends with Nicaea (325).

trads.d: From the Council of Nicaea (325) to the East–West schism: the Trinity was defined, monasticism spread from Egypt, and Christianity became the state religion (380).
trads.an: Council of Nicaea 325; Edict of Thessalonica 380.

trads.d: Arius taught that the Son was created by and subordinate to the Father. It was rejected at Nicaea, but Germanic kingdoms held it for centuries.
trads.an: Arius (c. 256–336) was denounced by an Alexandrian synod in 321 and condemned at Nicaea (325); Ulfilas evangelized the Goths, who converted c. 376; Vandals, Visigoths (to 589) and Lombards were Arian, and Garibald (671) was the last Arian king. Start moved from 318 to 321 and end from 700 to 671. Scholars call 'Arian controversy' a misnomer.

trads.d: Led by the Pope in Rome, Catholicism has seven sacraments, veneration of saints and Mary, religious orders and celibate Latin priests (mandatory from 1139). It is the largest Christian church, with over a billion members.
trads.an: East–West schism 1054; Second Lateran Council mandated clerical celibacy in 1139.

trads.d: A communion of self-governing churches (Constantinople, Moscow, Greece and others) that venerates icons and keeps Byzantine liturgy. Parish priests may marry before ordination.
trads.an: East–West schism 1054.
kt: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom

trads.d: The Coptic, Syriac, Malankara and Eritrean churches rejected the Council of Chalcedon (451) and hold a 'miaphysite' view: one united nature of Christ.
trads.an: Council of Chalcedon 451.

trads.d: Aksum adopted Christianity around 330. The church keeps Saturday alongside Sunday, avoids meats deemed unclean and fasts about 250 days a year. Every church must hold a tabot, a replica of the Ark. It became self-governing in 1959 and has about 60 million members.
trads.an: Aksum Christianized c. 330, autocephaly 1959, about 60 million adherents worldwide; Saturday kept alongside Sunday; a tabot in every church; unclean meats avoided; about 250 fast days a year. Circumcision is a cultural custom, not a religious requirement (the liturgy rejects circumcision 'like the Jews'), so that trait was removed and the description fixed.

trads.d: Armenia was the first kingdom to adopt Christianity (traditionally 301). The church keeps the matagh, a blessed animal offering shared with the poor.
trads.an: Tiridates III made Christianity the state religion 'between 300 and 301' by tradition; estimates range from 284 to 314 (Garsoïan favors 314). About 9 million adherents (church figure). The matagh offering is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Called 'Nestorian' by its rivals, the Church of the East declared independence from western churches in 424 and sent missions along the Silk Road to China (635) and India. It continues as the Assyrian and Ancient Churches of the East.
trads.an: Declared independence in 424 under Catholicos Dadishoʿ, and already a separate organization by 431, so start moved from 431 to 424. Reached China in 635 (Alopen); Xi'an Stele 781; successors are the Assyrian and Ancient Churches of the East. Aniconism became the norm but was not absolute.

trads.d: Missionaries reached Chang'an in 635. The Xi'an Stele (781) presents Christian ideas in Buddhist and Daoist terms.
trads.an: Alopen reached Chang'an in 635; the Xi'an Stele was erected on 7 January 781.

trads.d: Marcion rejected the Hebrew Bible's God as a lesser, harsh creator distinct from the loving Father revealed by Jesus. He compiled the first Christian canon.
trads.an: The checked source says Marcion preached in Rome c. 150; 144 is the traditional date of his break with the Roman church. Some scholars do not class him as Gnostic.

trads.d: The 'New Prophecy' of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla claimed ongoing ecstatic revelation from the Holy Spirit.
trads.an: Founded by Montanus with Prisca and Maximilla. The start date is debated (c. 135–177 CE); the movement persisted locally into the 6th c. (Justinian's measures 530–550; Tascodrugites c. 600).
kt: Oracles of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla

trads.d: A North African church that held that sacraments from clergy who had lapsed under persecution were invalid.
trads.an: Donatist schism 311–314 (the checked timeline gives 314 for the formal condemnation).

trads.r: Piedmont, Italy, and the Río de la Plata
trads.d: Followers of Peter Waldo preached apostolic poverty and the Bible in the common language. They joined the Reformation in 1532.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Peter Waldo 1140–1205.

trads.d: Followers of John Wycliffe, who translated the Bible into English and attacked clerical wealth and transubstantiation.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: John Wycliffe (1320s–1384).

trads.d: After Jan Hus was burned in 1415, Bohemian reformers demanded communion in both kinds (bread and wine) and church reform.
trads.an: Jan Hus executed during the Council of Constance (1414–18).

trads.d: The Unitas Fratrum, refounded at Herrnhut in 1722, pioneered Protestant world missions.
trads.an: Renewal at Herrnhut under Zinzendorf in 1722.

trads.d: Martin Luther's protest of 1517 taught salvation by grace through faith alone and the authority of scripture alone, with married pastors.
trads.an: 95 Theses 1517.

trads.d: Zwingli (Zurich, 1523) and Calvin (Geneva, 1536) stripped churches of images and taught God's sovereign predestination.
trads.an: Zwingli began reform preaching in Zurich in 1519 (council adopted it in 1523); Calvin's Geneva from 1536/1541.

trads.d: Reformed churches governed by elected elders (presbyters), shaped by John Knox and the Scottish Reformation of 1560.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: John Knox (1510–1572).

trads.d: Each local congregation is self-governing. This was the tradition of the Puritans and Pilgrims of New England.
trads.an: Rooted in Elizabethan Separatism; Robert Browne set out congregational principles (Holland 1581); the Pilgrims brought it to Plymouth in 1620; self-governing congregations; Cambridge Platform (1648) and Savoy Declaration (1658); continued by the United Church of Christ and others.

trads.d: Radical reformers who baptized adult believers only (Zurich, 1525), separated church from state and refused to bear arms.
trads.an: Believer's baptism; associated with pacifism.

trads.r: Netherlands, then the Americas and Africa
trads.d: Followers of Menno Simons. They are known for peace witness, relief service and simple living.
trads.an: Menno Simons left Catholicism in 1536 (died 1561).

trads.d: Anabaptists who share all property in farming colonies, following Jakob Hutter.
trads.an: Communes formed in 1528 in Tyrol; near-total community of goods; 58,392 people in 544 colonies (2024).

trads.d: Jakob Ammann's 1693 split from the Swiss Mennonites. They live in plain-dress communities that limit modern technology.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Jakob Ammann (1656–1730).

trads.d: The Church of England split from Rome under Henry VIII (1534). It keeps bishops and a liturgical tradition while holding Protestant doctrine, and spread worldwide as the Anglican Communion.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556) among Anglicanism's founders.

trads.d: John and Charles Wesley's revival stressed a felt experience of grace, holy living and social reform.
trads.an: Wesley's Aldersgate experience 1738; field preaching from 1739.
kt: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament

trads.d: Baptists practise believer's baptism by immersion, keep each congregation independent and hold to soul liberty. They began with English Separatists in Amsterdam in 1609.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: John Smyth (1570–1612).

trads.d: George Fox taught that the 'inner light' of Christ is in everyone. Quakers worship in waiting silence without clergy or sacraments, and are known for their peace testimony and abolitionism.
trads.an: The checked timeline dates George Fox's movement to 1648; 1652 (Pendle Hill vision) is the conventional founding year; both noted.

trads.d: Unitarians reject the Trinity and see Jesus as fully human. The Edict of Torda (1568) protected Unitarians in Transylvania.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Michael Servetus (1511?–1553) as precursor.

trads.d: A creedless merger (1961) of Unitarians and Universalists that draws on many religions and on humanism.
trads.an: The UUA formed in May 1961 from the American Unitarian Association (1825) and the Universalist Church of America (1793); creedless ('deeds, not creeds'); the seven principles (1960) were replaced in 2024 by values centred on love; about 1.4 million Americans identify as UU (2025).

trads.d: A Protestant movement of the Great Awakenings stressing conversion ('born again'), biblical authority, the cross and activism.
trads.an: The Great Awakenings were evangelical revival periods.

trads.d: Barton Stone and the Campbells sought to restore New Testament Christianity. It produced the Churches of Christ and the Disciples of Christ.
trads.an: Begun in the Second Great Awakening; Stone's and the Campbells' movements united by handshake in Lexington in 1832; weekly communion, believer's immersion, no creeds; Churches of Christ, Disciples of Christ and independent Christian churches.

trads.d: William Miller predicted Christ's return in 1844. The 'Great Disappointment' that followed gave rise to Adventism.
trads.an: William Miller began the Adventist movement in the 1830s.
kt: Millerite charts and periodicals (Signs of the Times)

trads.d: Adventists keep the Saturday Sabbath, follow health laws (many are vegetarian), teach that the dead sleep until the resurrection, and expect Christ's soon return. Ellen G. White is regarded as a prophet.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: James White (1821–1881) and Ellen G. White (1827–1915).
kt: writings of Ellen G. White (The Great Controversy)

trads.d: Founded on Charles Russell's Bible Student movement (Zion's Watch Tower, 1879), Witnesses are non-trinitarian, preach door to door, remain politically neutral and do not celebrate birthdays or Christmas.
trads.an: Zion's Watch Tower started 1879; the name Jehovah's Witnesses was adopted in 1931.

trads.d: Joseph Smith's restoration, with the Book of Mormon (1830), modern prophets and temples, during the Second Great Awakening.
trads.an: Church of Christ founded 6 April 1830 (Book of Mormon published 1830).

trads.n: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
trads.d: Led after the 1844 succession crisis by Brigham Young to Utah. It has a lay priesthood, temples, the Word of Wisdom (no alcohol, tobacco, coffee or tea) and tithing, and reports over 17 million members.
trads.an: Brigham Young led the largest group to Utah after the 1844 succession crisis; c. 17 million members (church reports over 16 million).

trads.d: The 'Reorganized' Latter Day Saint church, led by Joseph Smith III, now close to mainline Protestantism. It ordains women.
trads.an: Reorganized Church formed in 1860 under Joseph Smith III, later renamed Community of Christ.

trads.d: Mary Baker Eddy taught that God is Mind, matter is illusion, and illness is healed through prayer.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Mary Baker Eddy (1821–1910).
kt: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures

trads.d: Holiness churches teach entire sanctification as a second work of grace. The Church of the Nazarene and the Wesleyans belong to this movement.
trads.an: Emerged within 19th-c. Methodism.
kt: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection (Wesley)

trads.d: The Azusa Street Revival (1906) spread speaking in tongues, divine healing and prophecy. It is the fastest-growing Christian movement of the 20th century.
trads.an: Parham's Bethel Bible School students reported tongues on 1 January 1901; Azusa Street Revival from April 1906; c. 279 million classical Pentecostals (Pew, 2011), over 644 million including charismatics.

trads.d: Pentecostal-style gifts of the Spirit adopted inside older churches from 1960, including Catholic charismatic renewal.
trads.an: Pentecostalism gave rise to the charismatic movement in established denominations.

trads.d: Old Believers rejected Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms of 1652–66 and kept the older Russian rites. They have often been persecuted.
trads.an: Nikon's reforms and the Raskol 1653–1666; Avvakum burned 1682.

trads.d: 23 churches with Eastern rites in full communion with Rome, about 18 million members in all. The Syro-Malabar Church is the largest and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church (Union of Brest, 1595) the second largest. The Maronites never fully separated.
trads.an: 23 Eastern Catholic churches in full communion with Rome, with about 18 million members (2023). The Syro-Malabar Church is the largest and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church second (earlier wording implied otherwise). The Maronites are treated as never having fully separated. Most allow married priests. Description updated.
kt: Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990)
kf: patriarchs of the sui iuris churches

trads.d: Catholics who rejected papal infallibility (1870), joined with the Church of Utrecht. They allow married clergy.
trads.an: The Old Catholic movement formed after Vatican I (1870), joining the Church of Utrecht, which had been independent since the early 18th c.

trads.d: The United Society of Believers broke from the Quakers around 1747. Ann Lee was revealed in 1770 as Christ's second appearing. Members lived in celibate communities and worshipped through ecstatic, later choreographed, dance. Three members remained at Sabbathday Lake, Maine, as of 2025.
trads.an: Founded c. 1747 by the Wardleys after breaking from the Quakers; Ann Lee recognized in 1770 as Christ's second appearing; celibacy; ecstatic, later choreographed, dance. Three members as of 2025 after one joined Sabbathday Lake in August 2025; description updated.

trads.d: John Thomas founded them. They are non-trinitarian, believe the soul is mortal, refuse military service and await Christ's kingdom on earth.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: John Thomas (1805–1871).

trads.d: William and Catherine Booth's evangelical army, with military ranks, social service and no sacraments.
trads.an: Salvation Army 1865.

trads.d: A non-trinitarian church founded by Felix Manalo. It holds that it is the restored true church and votes as a bloc.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Felix Manalo (1886–1963).

trads.d: Simon Kimbangu was a healer and prophet, imprisoned by Belgian authorities. Kimbanguism is one of Africa's largest independent churches.
trads.an: Kimbangu's healing ministry began in April 1921; jailed by Belgian authorities until his death in 1951; alcohol, tobacco, polygamy and dancing prohibited; the church holds Kimbangu to be the Holy Spirit (controversial); Baptist roots; c. 6 million by church estimate.

trads.d: Yoruba 'praying' churches, such as the Cherubim and Seraphim and the Church of the Lord, that stress healing prayer, visions and white garments.
trads.an: Developed in SW Nigeria from c. 1918 amid health crises; Cherubim and Seraphim (1925), Church of the Lord (1930), Christ Apostolic Church revival (1930); prayer, faith healing and visions. White garments not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Founded in 1910 by Engenas Lekganyane and one of the largest African-initiated churches in southern Africa (about 5 million members in 2001). It stresses faith healing and abstinence from alcohol and tobacco, and holds an Easter pilgrimage to Moria attended by up to a million.
trads.an: Founded in 1910 by Engenas Lekganyane (not 1924); 4.97 million members in the 2001 census; healing, no alcohol or tobacco, Easter pilgrimage to Moria. Called 'one of the largest' (not 'the largest') African-initiated churches. Pork and ancestor claims not confirmed, so those traits were removed.

trads.d: Evangelical believers in Jesus who keep Jewish practices. Most Jewish bodies regard it as a form of Christianity.
trads.an: Grew from 19th-c. Hebrew Christian missions; took shape in the US in the 1960s–70s; Jews for Jesus founded in 1973; considered a form of Christianity by all mainstream Jewish movements; about 175,000–250,000 in the US and some 30,000 in Israel.

trads.d: Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was Jesus's younger brother, led a revolution that killed millions and was crushed in 1864.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Hong Xiuquan (1814–1864).
kt: Good Words for Exhorting the Age (Liang Fa)

trads.d: Sun Myung Moon's Divine Principle hails him and his wife as the 'True Parents' who complete Christ's mission. The church is known for mass weddings.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Sun Myung Moon (1920–2012).

trads.d: Russian 'Spirit Wrestlers', first recorded in 1701, rejected priests and icons, believing God dwells in every person. About 7,000 burned their weapons in 1895, and some 7,500 emigrated to Canada in 1899.
trads.an: First recorded in 1701 (origins uncertain); rejected priests and icons; c. 7,000 burned weapons in 1895; c. 7,500 reached Canada in 1899; vegetarian by the late 1880s. 1,675 self-identified in Canada's 2021 census. Start moved from 1700 to 1701.

trads.d: Emanuel Swedenborg's visions of heaven, hell and spiritual 'correspondences'. He taught that God is one person, revealed as Jesus.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772).

trads.d: Muhammad's revelations (from 610, collected as the Qur'an) proclaimed one God, the final judgment and a community bound by prayer, almsgiving, fasting and pilgrimage. Within a century Islam stretched from Spain to Central Asia.
trads.an: The first Islamic state was founded in Medina in 622; the Rashidun caliphs ruled 632–661; by 750 Muslim rule ran from Hispania to Sind and Central Asia.

trads.d: Sunnis follow the Prophet's custom (sunna) as transmitted in hadith collections, accept the first four caliphs, and are organized through four schools of law. They are about 85–90% of the world's two billion Muslims.
trads.an: 85–90% of Muslims; four law schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi, Hanbali).

trads.d: The 'party of Ali' holds that leadership passed through the Prophet's family. The martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala (680) is mourned each Ashura.
trads.an: Split over the succession; Karbala; about 10–13% of Muslims, of whom c. 85% are Twelvers.

trads.d: The largest Shia branch. Twelvers believe the twelfth Imam went into occultation in 874 and will return as the Mahdi, and are guided meanwhile by senior jurists.
trads.an: About 85% of Shia are Twelvers.

trads.r: South Asia, Central Asia, East Africa
trads.d: Ismailis follow a living line of imams. They read the Qur'an's inner meaning (bāṭin) through Neoplatonic thought, and their Fatimid caliphate ruled Egypt from 909 to 1171.
trads.an: Imamate through Jaʿfar al-Sadiq's line; bāṭinī esotericism. The 765 split date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.r: Worldwide, led by the Aga Khan
trads.d: Nizaris follow a living imam, the Aga Khan. Their medieval mountain state centered on Alamut.
trads.an: Nizari–Mustaʿli split noted; the 1094 date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: The Dawoodi Bohras and related groups, led by a Dāʿī in the absence of the hidden imam.
trads.an: Nizari–Mustaʿli split noted; the 1094 date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Druze teaching emerged from Fatimid Ismailism in 1017. Druze await the return of the caliph al-Ḥākim from occultation, but their texts warn against deifying any human. They believe in immediate reincarnation and have been closed to converts since the 1040s. They do not identify as Muslims.
trads.an: Divine call opened 30 May 1017; new pledges ended 1043 and conversion closed by 1046; reincarnation only into human bodies; c. 0.8–1 million adherents (up to 2 million). Al-Hakim is awaited from occultation, but Druze texts warn against treating any human as God, so the 'divine incarnation' trait was removed and the description reworded. Druze do not identify as Muslims (Ismaili origin noted).

trads.d: Zaydis accept any learned descendant of the Prophet who rises up as imam. They are closest to Sunnis in law.
trads.an: Named after Zayd ibn Ali; details not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: An esoteric faith (Nusayri) from Ibn Nusayr. It teaches a triad of Ali, Muhammad and Salman, as well as reincarnation.
trads.an: Ibn Nusayr (d. c. 868); triad of Ali (Maʿna), Muhammad (Ism) and Salman (Bab); reincarnation; c. 2–3 million worldwide.

trads.d: Anatolian Alevis love Ali and the Twelve Imams. They worship in cem gatherings with the semah dance and music, with men and women together, rather than in mosques.
trads.an: Roots in Seljuk-era (11th–12th c.) Turkmen Sufi, pro-Alid Islam; the start date of 1500 marks the Safavid-era crystallization of Kizilbash identity. Cem with semah performed by men and women together; worship in the cemevi; linked to Haji Bektash; c. 4–15% of Turkey (some estimates 20–25 million).

trads.d: 'Those who went out' rejected Ali's arbitration (657). They held that any pious Muslim could be caliph and that grave sinners were apostates.
trads.an: Broke away during the First Fitna.

trads.d: The moderate surviving Kharijite branch, the majority in Oman.
trads.an: Ibadis listed; Oman majority not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Islamic mysticism: remembrance of God (dhikr), master–disciple lineages, saints' shrines and the love poetry of Rumi and Hafez. Ibn Arabi taught the 'unity of being'.
trads.an: Usually dated to early Islam, partly as an ascetic reaction under the Umayyads (Hasan al-Basri, d. 728), so start moved from 750 to 700; dhikr, silsila, Ibn Arabi's wahdat al-wujud; samāʿ.

trads.d: Followers of Rumi, famous for the sama ceremony of the whirling dervishes.
trads.an: Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes'.

trads.d: A Sufi order named after Haji Bektash Veli (13th c.) with heterodox features such as reverence for Ali and ritual use of rakia. It was the Janissaries' order until banned in 1826, and has had its world center in Tirana since 1930.
trads.an: Evolved in 13th-c. Anatolia, rituals systematized by Balım Sultan (1509–16); official order of the Janissaries, banned 1826; headquarters in Tirana from 1930; ritual use of rakia ('dem'). A formal Allah–Muhammad–Ali triad is not described in the checked source, so that trait was removed.

trads.d: Muʿin al-Din Chishti's order at Ajmer (around 1200), known for qawwali music and openness to all.
trads.an: Moinuddin Chishti (1141–1236) settled at Ajmer; the Chishtiyya use samāʿ but prohibit dancing with intent.

trads.d: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab's 1744 pact with the House of Saud launched a movement to purge saint veneration and shrine pilgrimage as shirk and return to the early generations (salaf). Followers reject the label 'Wahhabi' and call themselves Salafi or Muwahhidun.
trads.an: 1744 pact with Muhammad bin Saud; condemned saint veneration and shrine pilgrimage as shirk; often treated as a subset of Salafism. 'Wahhabi' is an exonym that followers reject, and the entry is renamed accordingly.

trads.d: A revivalist Hanafi seminary movement founded at Deoband, India, in 1866.
trads.an: Deobandi movement listed; the 1866 date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: A South Asian Sunni movement that defends saint veneration and celebrates the Prophet's birthday. Ahmed Raza Khan led it.
