trads.an: Barelvi movement listed; founder not named in the checked source.

trads.d: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claimed to be the promised Messiah and Mahdi and taught 'jihad of the pen'. Many Muslims do not accept Ahmadis as Muslims, and they are persecuted in Pakistan.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908).

trads.d: The Báb ('the Gate') proclaimed a new revelation in 1844. He was executed in 1850 and his followers were massacred.
trads.an: The Báb began teaching in 1844 and was executed in 1850.

trads.d: Bahá'u'lláh (1863) taught that one God has sent successive messengers, among them Abraham, Krishna, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad. It teaches the unity of humanity and equality of women and men. Elected assemblies replace clergy, with the Universal House of Justice at the top. Alcohol is forbidden, a daily prayer is obligatory and there is a 19-day fast. About 7–8 million adherents.
trads.an: The Báb began teaching in 1844 and was executed in 1850; Baháʼu'lláh's 1863 claim; progressive revelation; elected assemblies and the Universal House of Justice with no clergy; alcohol forbidden; Nineteen-Day Fast; daily obligatory prayer; c. 7–8 million adherents.

trads.d: Noble Drew Ali taught that Black Americans are 'Moorish' and Muslim. He wrote the Circle Seven Koran.
trads.an: Founded in 1913 in Newark by Noble Drew Ali; a key source for the Nation of Islam. The Circle Seven Koran is not covered by the checked source.
kt: Circle Seven Koran (Holy Koran of the Moorish Science Temple)

trads.d: Founded in Detroit in 1930 by Wallace Fard Muhammad, whom it teaches was God in person, and led by Elijah Muhammad and later Louis Farrakhan. It preaches Black self-reliance, forbids pork, alcohol and tobacco, and rejects any afterlife. Malcolm X left in 1964 for Sunni Islam.
trads.an: Founded July 1930 in Detroit by Wallace Fard Muhammad, who is taught to be God in person; Elijah Muhammad; Farrakhan rebuilt it in 1977; Malcolm X left in March 1964; pork, alcohol and tobacco forbidden. The Nation rejects any afterlife, so judgment/soul traits were removed and materialism added.
kt: Message to the Blackman in America

trads.d: Emperor Akbar's small court discipleship (1582), with only 19 known members, blended devotion to God and the emperor with light and fire veneration and vegetarianism. Scholars debate whether it was a religion at all.
trads.an: Founded 1582 at Fatehpur Sikri; defunct c. 1605; only 19 identified followers; sun and light veneration with a fire ritual; vegetarianism. Scholars debate whether it was a religion or a discipleship around Akbar. Fire trait added.

trads.r: Alexandria, then Renaissance Europe and modern esotericism
trads.d: Teachings attributed to 'Hermes Trismegistus' (Corpus Hermeticum, 1st–3rd c.) on knowing God through the mind, alchemy and astrology. They were rediscovered by Ficino in 1463.
trads.an: Ficino translated part of the Corpus Hermeticum (Lazzarelli the rest); the exact 1463 date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Sethians taught that an ignorant creator, Yaldabaoth, trapped divine sparks in matter, and that knowledge (gnosis) frees them. Texts such as the Apocryphon of John survive in the Nag Hammadi library.
trads.an: Major Gnostic current of the 2nd–3rd c.; Apocryphon of John; Yaldabaoth.

trads.d: Valentinus's Christian gnosticism of aeons and the fallen Sophia, the most influential gnostic school.
trads.an: Valentinus c. 100–180; Sophia gives birth to the demiurge.

trads.d: The last surviving gnostic religion of antiquity. Mandaeans revere John the Baptist as their greatest prophet and immerse in flowing water every Sunday, and they await the soul's ascent to the World of Light. Many scholars accept a Judean origin and 1st-century migration, as the community holds; others place it later. About 60,000–100,000 remain.
trads.an: Origins are debated: many scholars argue for a Judean/Israelite origin with migration in the 1st c. CE (the community's own account), while others place it later (van Bladel: no earlier than the 5th c.). John the Baptist is the greatest and final prophet but not the founder (Adam is); masbuta immersion every Sunday; Ptahil only partly a demiurge; no converts; c. 60,000–100,000 adherents.

trads.d: An Armenian dualist Christian movement that rejected icons, saints and hierarchy. The Byzantines fought it as heresy.
trads.an: Flourished 650–872, so end moved from 900 to 872.

trads.d: Bulgarian dualists, followers of the priest Bogomil, who taught that the material world was Satan's creation.
trads.an: Emerged in Bulgaria between 927 and 970.

trads.d: Dualists with ascetic perfecti and the consolamentum rite. The Albigensian Crusade (1209–29) and the Inquisition destroyed them.
trads.an: Albigensian Crusade 1209–1229.

trads.d: The Fama Fraternitatis (1614) announced a secret brotherhood of Christian-Hermetic sages. Many later orders claim that lineage.
trads.an: Rosicrucian manifestos published 1614–1616.

trads.d: A fraternal order, not a religion, that requires belief in a Supreme Being. Its symbolic initiations (Grand Lodge, 1717) shaped many later movements.
trads.an: The checked source traces Freemasonry as an initiatory brotherhood to late-16th-c. Scotland; 1717 marks the first Grand Lodge (London). Both noted.

trads.d: Emerson and Thoreau found the divine in nature and intuition, reading the Upanishads alongside the Bible.
trads.an: Transcendental Club founded 12 September 1836; grew from Harvard Unitarianism; Thoreau at Walden (1845; Walden published 1854); Eastern texts (Gita, Upanishads); faded after c. 1850 with a later second wave.

trads.d: A movement holding that right thinking heals and prospers. Unity Church and Religious Science belong to it.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Phineas Quimby (1802–1866).

trads.d: Spiritualism began with the Fox sisters' 'rappings' (1848) and centers on communication with the dead through mediums and séances.
trads.an: Emerged in the United States in the 1840s.

trads.d: Allan Kardec's Spirits' Book (1857) joined mediumship with reincarnation and charity. It is huge in Brazil.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Allan Kardec (1804–1869).

trads.r: New York, then India and worldwide
trads.d: Helena Blavatsky and Henry Olcott's society taught a hidden 'ancient wisdom' behind all religions, with karma, reincarnation and Masters. It brought Asian ideas to the West.
trads.an: Founded in New York City in 1875 by Blavatsky, Olcott and Judge; Masters; karma and reincarnation; popularized Asian ideas in the West and aided the Buddhist and Hindu revivals.

trads.d: Rudolf Steiner's Christian 'spiritual science'. It inspired Waldorf schools and biodynamic farming.
trads.an: Steiner founded the Anthroposophical Society on 28 December 1912 and was expelled from the Theosophical Society in March 1913.

trads.n: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
trads.d: A ceremonial magic order (1888) that synthesized Kabbalah, tarot and Hermeticism.
trads.an: Founded in the late 19th c.

trads.d: Aleister Crowley's religion from The Book of the Law (1904): 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law'.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Aleister Crowley (1875–1947).
kt: The Book of the Law (Liber AL vel Legis)

trads.d: Gerald Gardner made modern witchcraft public in 1954. Covens honor a Goddess and a God, and celebrate the eight-festival Wheel of the Year. The Wiccan Rede says 'An it harm none, do what ye will'.
trads.an: Wheel of the Year (eight festivals) and Goddess/God duotheism confirmed; Gardner claimed initiation in 1939 and publicized Wicca in 1954.
kf: the Goddess and the Horned God

trads.d: A loose movement of spiritual self-development, channeling, crystals and holistic healing. It draws eclectically on Theosophy, Asian religions and Indigenous traditions.
trads.an: New Age phenomenon from the 1970s, a named movement by the 1980s.

trads.d: Hymns of the Rigveda praised Indra, Agni and Soma. Brahmin priests performed fire sacrifices (yajña) to sustain the cosmic order (ṛta), and the Vedas were passed down orally with great precision.
trads.an: Vedic period c. 1500–500 BCE (variants 1750–500); Rigveda c. 1500–1200 BCE, transmitted orally until the 4th c. CE.

trads.d: Forest teachers turned ritual inward. The self (ātman) is identical to ultimate reality (Brahman), and knowledge frees one from karma and rebirth.
trads.an: Earliest Upanishads 9th–8th c. BCE; karma and reincarnation in the classical period (800–200 BCE).

trads.d: A synthesis took shape between about 200 BCE and 500 CE: temple worship (pūjā) of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess, the epics and Purāṇas, avatars, cosmic ages and the duties of dharma. It is the shared base of most Hindu sects. About 1.2 billion Hindus today.
trads.an: 'Hindu synthesis' from c. 500–200 BCE to 300–500 CE; first Puranas under the Guptas (c. 320–650).

trads.d: Devotion to Shiva as the supreme god, from Pāśupata ascetics to Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta.
trads.an: Developed through bhakti in the classical period.

trads.d: Devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, especially Krishna and Rama. The Heliodorus pillar (around 113 BCE) is early evidence.
trads.an: Developed through bhakti in the classical period.

trads.d: Worship of the Goddess (Devī, Durgā, Kālī) as the supreme power (śakti), celebrated in the Devī Māhātmya.
trads.an: Shakti/Devi is a principal Puranic deity; Shaktism as a named tradition is not dated in the checked source.

trads.d: A tradition associated with Adi Shankara that worships five deities equally (pañcāyatana) as forms of one Brahman.
trads.an: Credited to Shankara, with mathas at Sringeri, Kanchi, Puri, Dwarka and Jyotir; five-deity pañcāyatana pūjā.

trads.d: Non-dualism, taught by Gauḍapāda and Shankara: Brahman alone is real, and the world of difference is māyā. It has monastic seats (mathas) and is very influential in modern Hinduism.
trads.an: Shankara (8th c.) systematized Advaita, though his fame grew later via Vidyaranya (14th c.).

trads.d: Ramanuja's 'qualified non-dualism': souls and the world are real parts of a personal God, reached by devotion and surrender.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Ramanuja 1017–1137.

trads.d: Madhva's dualism held that God, souls and matter are eternally distinct. He uniquely taught that some souls are eternally damned.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Madhvacharya 1238–1317.

trads.d: Poet-saints, including women and low-caste devotees, sang passionate love for Vishnu (Āḻvārs, 3rd–9th c.) and Shiva (Nāyaṉārs, 4th–10th c.). This sparked the bhakti movement across India.
trads.an: Alvars dated 3rd–9th c. and Nayanars 4th–10th c. CE (traditional Alvar dates far earlier); start moved from 600 to 300 and end from 900 to 1000.

trads.d: Kabir, Ravidas and others worshipped a formless God through the divine Name, rejecting idols, caste and the claims of both Hindu and Muslim religious authorities.
trads.an: Sant Mat: 14th–17th c. reform movement of poet-sants including Kabir.

trads.d: Chaitanya taught ecstatic chanting (kīrtana) of Krishna's names, with Krishna as the Supreme Lord.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu 1486–1534.

trads.d: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami brought Gauḍīya devotion to the West in New York in 1966.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada (1896–1977).

trads.d: Basava's movement rejected caste and temple ritual. Each devotee wears a personal linga.
trads.an: Established by Basavanna in the 12th c.

trads.d: A non-dual Tantric Shaivism, from Vasugupta's Shiva Sutras to Abhinavagupta.
trads.an: Vasugupta and lineage, including Abhinavagupta.

trads.d: Esoteric initiatory traditions using mantra, maṇḍala and ritual to harness divine power. It shaped Hindu, Buddhist and Jain practice from about the 5th–6th centuries.
trads.an: Tantra appears in the post-Gupta period; no start date in the checked source.

trads.d: Gorakhnath's yogis, who developed haṭha yoga.
trads.an: Siddha Siddhanta following Gorakhnath and Matsyendranath.

trads.d: The Yoga Sūtras (dated between the 2nd c. BCE and the 5th c. CE) set out an eight-limbed path of ethics, posture, breath and meditation to free spirit from matter.
trads.an: Yoga codified among the philosophical schools in the early centuries CE; the Yoga Sutras date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Followers of Sahajanand Swami (Swaminarayan). It is known for strict ethics and grand temples, the BAPS mandirs.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Swaminarayan (1781–1830).

trads.d: Ram Mohan Roy's reform movement for monotheistic, image-free Hinduism, against sati and caste.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833).

trads.d: Dayananda Saraswati's 'back to the Vedas' movement rejected idols and birth caste and promoted the fire rite (havan).
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Dayananda Saraswati (1824–1883).

trads.d: Vivekananda spread Ramakrishna's teaching that all religions are paths to one truth, speaking at Chicago in 1893.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902).

trads.d: Followers of Ayya Vaikundar, who opposed caste oppression. Worshippers use a mirror instead of an idol.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Ayya Vaikundar (1833–1851).

trads.d: A Shaiva–Buddhist–Austronesian blend with daily offerings (canang), temple festivals and ancestor rites.
trads.an: Shiva-centred worship with Buddhist elements and Austronesian ancestor veneration; Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa; daily canang sari offerings; odalan temple festivals and Galungan every 210 days; ngaben cremation. About 3.8 million adherents. Legend credits Rsi Markandeya (8th c.), with Majapahit conquest in 1343 and Nirartha's reforms from 1492.

trads.d: Wandering renouncers of the mid-1st millennium BCE who sought release from rebirth through austerity and insight, often challenging brahmin ritual authority. Whether the movement was 'non-Vedic' is debated. Buddhism, Jainism and the Ājīvikas came from this milieu.
trads.an: The śramaṇa tradition arose from the mid-1st millennium BCE, with some movements earlier. The 'non-Vedic' framing is disputed (Olivelle), so the description is softened.
kt: Early Buddhist and Jain texts describing the śramaṇas

trads.d: An Indian materialist school that denied gods, karma and an afterlife and accepted only perception as knowledge. It is known mainly through its critics.
trads.an: Materialist school (Ajita Kesakambalī) denying afterlife, rebirth and karma.

trads.d: Makkhali Gosāla taught that fate (niyati) rules everything, and his followers practised extreme austerity.
trads.an: Founded by Makkhali Gosāla in the 5th c. BCE; niyati determinism; persisted in South India until the 14th c.

trads.d: Mahāvīra, the 24th Tīrthaṅkara, taught strict non-violence, non-possessiveness and many-sidedness (anekāntavāda). Karma is a fine matter that clings to the soul (jīva) and is removed through austerity. Historians date Mahāvīra to the 5th c. BCE (Jain tradition: 599–527 BCE), and his predecessor Pārśva to the 8th–7th c. BCE.
trads.an: Historians place Mahāvīra in the 5th c. BCE as a contemporary of the Buddha (Dundas), and Pārśva in the 8th–7th c. BCE; Jain tradition gives 599–527 BCE. Start moved from 550 to 500 BCE, with both datings noted.

trads.d: 'Sky-clad' Jains, whose monks renounce all clothing and who hold that women cannot attain liberation without rebirth as men. Tradition ties the split to a famine under Bhadrabāhu (c. 300 BCE); Śvetāmbara accounts give 79/82 CE; many scholars place the final split later.
trads.an: Tradition ties the split to a 12-year famine under Bhadrabāhu, placed under Chandragupta Maurya (c. 324–297 BCE); Śvetāmbara accounts give 79/82 CE; scholars place the final split later. Digambaras hold that women cannot attain liberation and Śvetāmbaras that they can. Description notes both datings.

trads.d: 'White-clad' Jains, whose monks and nuns wear white. They accept that women can reach liberation.
trads.an: See Digambara: the split date is disputed; Śvetāmbaras hold that women can attain liberation.

trads.d: Jains who reject image worship and temples, building on Lonka Shah's 15th-century reform.
trads.an: Lonka Shah (15th c.) argued that the scriptures do not support temples or image worship; the sect was founded in the 17th c. by Lava of Surat; 32 Agamas; worship in sthanak halls.

trads.d: A reform order led by a single āchārya.
trads.an: Terapanth is named as aligned with Lonka's aniconic views; Acharya Bhikshu and the 1760 date are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Guru Nanak (1469–1539) proclaimed one formless God (Ik Onkar), equality of all, honest work and sharing. Sikh tradition dates his revelation to around 1499. Ten Gurus led the community until Guru Gobind Singh made the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Guru in 1708. It includes hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints such as Kabir and Baba Farid. Scholars place Sikhism within the bhakti milieu with some Sufi influence; Sikhs hold it to be a direct revelation. Langar, the free kitchen, feeds all comers. About 25–30 million Sikhs live today.
trads.an: Guru Nanak lived 1469–1539 and founded Kartarpur in 1526. The 1499 revelation date follows Sikh tradition. Khalsa 1699; Granth declared eternal Guru 1708; langar instituted by Guru Amar Das; Ik Onkar. Western scholars place Sikhism in the bhakti milieu with some Sufi influence, while Sikhs hold it to be a direct revelation and object to 'syncretic'; both views noted. 25–30 million adherents.

trads.d: A Sikh reform movement that follows a living Guru, wears white and is strictly vegetarian.
trads.an: Founded by Balak Singh and Ram Singh, who raised the white flag at Bhaini Sahib on 12 April 1857; a living Guru line (disputed by a rival faction); white dress; strict vegetarianism and no alcohol, tobacco or caffeine; the anti-colonial Kuka movement (66 executed in 1872).

trads.d: A 19th-century Sikh reform movement stressing the formless (nirankar) God and simple rites.
trads.an: Founded in 1851 near Rawalpindi by Baba Dyal Singh; formless God and no idols; nam simaran; hereditary living gurus; vegetarian, no alcohol or tobacco. Distinct from the later Sant Nirankari Mission.

trads.d: An ascetic order founded by Guru Nanak's son Sri Chand. It kept many Sikh shrines in the 18th century.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Sri Chand (1494–1629) founded the Udasi.

trads.d: A guru-led meditation path on the inner sound current (surat shabd yoga). Its largest branch is at Beas.
trads.an: Founded in 1861 when Shiv Dayal Singh began public discourses in Agra; surat shabd yoga under a living guru; strict lacto-vegetarianism and no alcohol; branches at Beas (1891) and Dayalbagh (1907).

trads.d: The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way between pleasure and austerity: no permanent self, and nirvana through ethics, meditation and wisdom. His dates are debated, from about 563–483 to 480–400 BCE.
trads.an: Buddha's birth c. 563 or c. 480 BCE, death between 411 and 400 BCE in recent dating; the start date of 450 BCE is a midpoint at medium confidence.

trads.d: The 'Elders' side of the first schism, over monastic rules, at or after the Second Council.
trads.an: First schism into Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika 'probably after the time of Ashoka', or at the Second Council (383 or c. 330 BCE).

trads.d: The 'Great Assembly' side of the first schism. Its ideas about the transcendent Buddha anticipate the Mahāyāna.
trads.an: Mahāsāṃghika and sub-groups (Lokottaravāda, Caitika and others).

trads.r: Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia
trads.d: The 'Teaching of the Elders' keeps the Pali Canon, written down in Sri Lanka around 29 BCE. Mahinda, Ashoka's son, brought it to Sri Lanka in the 3rd c. BCE.
trads.an: Mahinda brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka c. 250–220 BCE; Pali Canon written down in 29 BCE.

trads.d: Taught that dharmas (moments of experience) exist in past, present and future. Its Abhidharma shaped the Mahāyāna.
trads.an: Northwest India and Kashmir.

trads.d: A school that posited a 'person' (pudgala) that is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates.
trads.an: Sthavira offshoot founded by Vātsīputra, c. 3rd c. BCE.

trads.d: The 'Great Vehicle' holds up the bodhisattva who vows to free all beings. It teaches the emptiness of all things and buddha-nature, and the Lotus, Heart and other sutras. About 324 million Buddhists worldwide today, across all schools.
trads.an: Mahāyāna sutras date back to the 1st c. BCE.

trads.d: Nāgārjuna's 'Middle Way' philosophy: all things are empty of inherent existence.
trads.an: Nāgārjuna c. 150–250 CE.

trads.d: Asaṅga and Vasubandhu's 'mind-only' school, which analyzes how consciousness constructs experience.
trads.an: Founded in the 4th c. CE.

trads.d: Devotion to Amitābha Buddha, whose vow brings all who call his name to the Pure Land. Huiyuan's society (402) was an early center.
trads.an: Based on Amitābha veneration, with masters Tanluan (476–542), Daochuo and Shandao. Huiyuan's 402 society is the traditional starting point but is not covered by the checked source; noted.

trads.d: Hōnen (1175) taught reciting the nenbutsu, and Shinran taught faith alone. Shin priests marry. It is Japan's largest school.
trads.an: Hōnen (1133–1212) founded Pure Land as an independent sect.

trads.d: Chan stresses meditation and direct mind-to-mind transmission 'outside the scriptures'. It is traced to Bodhidharma (the traditional date) and Huineng.
trads.an: Bodhidharma settles at Shaolin in 527 (traditional).

trads.d: Eisai brought Rinzai koan practice to Japan in 1191 and Dōgen brought Sōtō 'just sitting' (zazen) in 1227.
trads.an: Dōgen brought Sōtō from China in 1227.

trads.d: Korean Chan, unified as the Jogye Order.
trads.an: Korean Seon derives from Chinese Chan.

trads.d: Vietnamese Chan blended with Pure Land. Thích Nhất Hạnh's 'engaged Buddhism' came from it.
trads.an: Vietnamese Thiền influenced by Chinese Chan.

trads.d: Zhiyi's systematic school based on the Lotus Sutra.
trads.an: Founded mainly by Zhiyi (538–597), based on the Lotus Sutra.

trads.d: Saichō brought Tiantai to Mount Hiei in 805. Many later Japanese founders trained there.
trads.an: Saichō went to China in 804 and founded Tendai on his return (805).

trads.d: Nichiren taught chanting 'Nam-myōhō-renge-kyō' and devotion to the Lotus Sutra alone.
trads.an: Nichiren born 1222; began preaching in 1253.

trads.d: A lay Nichiren movement with millions of members worldwide.
trads.an: Founded 1930.

trads.d: The 'Flower Garland' school of the interpenetration of all phenomena.
trads.an: Based on the Avataṃsaka Sutra; Dushun, Zhiyan, Fazang.

trads.d: Esoteric Buddhism of tantras, deity yoga, maṇḍalas and initiation by a guru (lama).
trads.an: Tantra, deity yoga, maṇḍalas and empowerment from a lama.

trads.d: Kūkai's esoteric school (806), centered on Mount Kōya.
trads.an: Kūkai went to China in 804 and founded Shingon on his return (806).

trads.d: The 'Ancient' school, traced to Padmasambhava and Samye monastery (around 779). It has married tantric practitioners and teaches Dzogchen.
trads.an: Traced to Padmasambhava and Śāntarakṣita, who built Samye in the late 8th c.; Dzogchen; lay ngagpa tantric specialists.
kt: terma texts incl. Tibetan Book of the Dead

trads.d: The lineage of Marpa, Milarepa and the Karmapas, centered on Mahāmudrā.
trads.an: Marpa introduced Sarma lineages in the 11th c.

trads.d: Founded at Sakya monastery in 1073. Its lamas ruled Tibet under the Mongols.
trads.an: Founded 1073; Sakya Pandita made viceroy of Central Tibet under the Mongols in 1249.

trads.d: Tsongkhapa's reformed school of the Dalai Lamas and Panchen Lamas, who are recognized as reincarnating lamas (tulkus).
trads.an: First Dalai Lama Gendun Drubpa (1391–1474).

trads.d: B. R. Ambedkar led hundreds of thousands of Dalits into Buddhism in 1956, reinterpreting it as a path of social liberation.
trads.an: Ambedkar's mass conversion in 1956.

trads.d: The Burmese lay meditation revival (Mahasi Sayadaw, S. N. Goenka), and from 1979 secular mindfulness programs, separated meditation from monastic ritual.
trads.an: 20th-century lay meditation movement.

trads.d: Huỳnh Phú Sổ's lay Buddhist reform: simple home worship, no temples or clergy.
trads.an: Founded 1939 by Huỳnh Phú Sổ.

trads.d: Sotaesan's modern Korean Buddhism, which venerates a simple circle (Il-Won-Sang) rather than statues.
trads.an: Korean reformed Buddhism (Wonbulgyo).

trads.d: Kings consulted ancestors and the high god Di through oracle bones and offered large-scale sacrifices, including humans.
trads.an: Ancestral gods and Shangdi linked to the Shang royal lineage.

trads.n: Zhou religion and the Mandate of Heaven
trads.d: Heaven (Tian) granted rule to virtuous kings and withdrew it from tyrants. Ancestor rites and ritual propriety (li) structured society.
trads.an: Tian as the transcendent moral source; the Mandate of Heaven ties rule to virtue.

trads.d: Worship of local gods (Mazu, Guan Yu), ancestors and immortals in temples, lineage halls and homes, with wu and tongji spirit mediums. By the Song dynasty it had blended Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist elements.
trads.an: Ancestor cults, territorial gods (Mazu, Guan Yu), wu and tongji mediums, and Song-era blending with Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism confirmed. The unsourced 'world's largest unorganized religion' claim was removed.

trads.d: Confucius (551–479 BCE) taught humaneness (ren), ritual propriety, filial piety and government by virtue. Scholars debate whether it is a religion, a philosophy or both.
trads.an: Confucius 551–479 BCE; ren, li, xiao; classed as religion or philosophy depending on definition; influential in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

trads.d: Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming integrated metaphysics, quiet sitting and self-cultivation, partly in answer to Buddhism.
trads.an: Developed in response to Buddhism and Taoism; Zhu Xi (Song) and Wang Yangming (Ming).
kt: Four Books with Zhu Xi's commentaries

trads.d: Mozi preached impartial care for all, opposed offensive war and luxury, and believed in Heaven's will and the spirits.
trads.an: Mozi's critique of Confucianism; Mohism later absorbed. Impartial care is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: The Daodejing and Zhuangzi teach harmony with the nameless Dao through effortless action (wu wei) and simplicity.
trads.an: The Daodejing existed by the 3rd c. BCE, perhaps growing from oral sayings; the Laozi legend developed in the Han and has no historical validity; wu wei and the unnamable Dao; commentaries by Wang Bi and Guo Xiang.

trads.n: Way of the Celestial Masters (Zhengyi Daoism)
trads.d: Zhang Daoling's revelation from the deified Laozi in 142 founded organized religious Daoism, with hereditary priests, healing, talismans and gods.
trads.an: Zhang Daoling's vision of Laozi in 142 CE; the movement developed from the Five Pecks of Rice at the end of the 2nd c.

trads.d: Revealed scriptures of visualization meditation (Shangqing) and universal salvation (Lingbao), partly modeled on Mahāyāna.
trads.an: Shangqing revelations 364–370 (Yang Xi); Lingbao scriptures compiled 397–402 by Ge Chaofu.

trads.d: The monastic 'Complete Perfection' school founded in 12th-century Shandong by Wang Chongyang (1113–1170), practicing internal alchemy. It is centered on the White Cloud Temple in Beijing.
trads.an: Founded in the 12th c. in Shandong by Wang Chongyang (1113–1170), so 1170 was his death year; start moved to 1167.

trads.d: Lay sects, already active in the Song dynasty, that awaited the future Buddha Maitreya and later worshipped the 'Unborn Venerable Mother'. They inspired several rebellions.
trads.an: White Lotus tradition already active in the Song dynasty. The deity is the 'Unborn Venerable Mother' (wording corrected from 'Eternal'). Mao Ziyuan (1133) is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: It grew from Wang Jueyi's 1870s sect, was renamed Yiguandao in 1905 and teaches that all five religions share one source, under the Unborn Mother. It was banned on the mainland after WWII and is large in Taiwan, where it was legalized in 1987.
trads.an: Derives from Wang Jueyi's Mohou Yizhu sect (1870s), renamed Yiguandao in 1905, banned on the mainland after WWII and registered in Taiwan in 1947, where salvationist movements together draw about 10% of the population. Start moved from 1930 to 1905.

trads.d: Ngô Văn Chiêu received séance messages from the Supreme Being (Cao Đài). The faith honors the Buddha, Laozi, Confucius, Jesus and Victor Hugo, under a pope-led hierarchy at Tây Ninh.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Ngô Văn Chiêu (1878–1926).
kt: Thánh Ngôn Hiệp Tuyển (collected spirit messages)

trads.d: Li Hongzhi's qigong-based practice of truthfulness, compassion and forbearance. It has been banned and persecuted in China since 1999.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Li Hongzhi (born 1951/52).

trads.d: Rice farmers brought rites for kami and clan ancestors. The early state rooted rule in the sun goddess Amaterasu.
trads.an: Kami veneration dates to the Yayoi period (300 BCE–250 CE); Buddhism arrived at the end of the Kofun period.

trads.d: The 'way of the kami': shrine worship, purification (harae, misogi) and festivals (matsuri). The Kojiki (712) records its myths. It was long blended with Buddhism.
trads.an: Kami; harae and misogi; matsuri; Kojiki 712; shinbutsu-shūgō; State Shinto formed in the Meiji era and separated from the state after 1945; about 100,000 shrines.

trads.d: Mountain ascetics (yamabushi) blending Shinto, esoteric Buddhism and Daoism, traced to En no Gyōja.
trads.an: Founded in the 7th c. with En no Gyōja as patriarch; yamabushi mountain ascetics; a syncretic mix of Esoteric Buddhism, Shinto, mountain worship and Taoism; banned in 1872 and revived after WWII.

trads.d: The Meiji state separated Shinto from Buddhism and built a cult of the divine emperor, dismantled in 1945.
trads.an: Meiji nationalists purged Buddhist elements and formed State Shinto; separated from the state after WWII.

trads.d: Nakayama Miki's revelations from 'God the Parent' teach the Joyous Life, with sacred dance and healing.
trads.an: Founded 1838 by Nakayama Miki.

trads.d: Konkō Daijin's mediation between people and one parent-like kami.
trads.an: Founded 1859 by Konkō Daijin.

trads.d: The prophetess Deguchi Nao began receiving revelations in 1892, and the group was organized with Deguchi Onisaburō by 1899. It was severely suppressed by the state in the 1920s–30s and influenced many later Japanese new religions.
trads.an: The checked table dates Ōmoto's formal founding to 1899; 1892 is when Deguchi Nao's revelations began. Both noted, and 1892 kept as the start of the movement. Severe state suppression in the 1930s confirmed.

trads.d: Mostly female shamans (mudang) perform gut rites with dance, possession and healing for clients and ancestors.
trads.an: Mudang are mostly women; gut rites with offerings, song, dance and (for kangsin-mu) possession. The earliest historical references date to the 12th c.; deeper origins are unclear, and some scholars resist calling ancient Korean religion 'shamanism'. Start kept at low confidence with this caveat.

trads.d: Choe Je-u's 'Eastern Learning' taught that 'humans are Heaven'. It fueled the Donghak peasant revolution of 1894.
trads.an: Choe Je-u began Donghak in 1860 as an alternative to 'Western Learning'; serving a person is serving Heaven (Haneullim); the 1894 peasant rebellion; renamed Cheondoism by Son Byong-hi on 1 December 1905; about 65,000 adherents (2015 census).

trads.d: San healers enter trance in all-night dances, with women clapping and singing and men dancing, to heal and battle illness. ǀKágge̥n the Mantis is the trickster-creator. Rock paintings in the Drakensberg, some about 3,000 years old, record such rites; the tradition is among the oldest continuing ones.
trads.an: Trance dance (women clap and sing, men dance) after initiation through a power animal such as the eland; ǀKágge̥n the Mantis trickster-demiurge; Drakensberg paintings c. 3,000 years old with religious meaning. The 'distant creator' ǃXu is likely a missionary-influenced figure, so the sky-god trait was removed and the rock-art age claim softened.

trads.d: Shared West and Central African patterns, reconstructed by comparison and very uncertain: a distant creator, many spirits, ancestors, divination and possession.
trads.an: High gods with lower gods, spirits and ancestors; diviners and healers; trance embodiment of deities and ancestors. (The 'distant' creator is a common scholarly characterization, not stated in this source.)

trads.d: Olódùmarè the creator, the Òrìṣà (Ọ̀ṣun, Ṣàngó, Ògún, Ọbàtálá), Ifá divination with its vast oral corpus, and ancestral rebirth. It is the source of Santería and Candomblé.
trads.an: Olódùmarè; Ọ̀ṣun, Ṣàngó, Ògún, Ọbàtálá; Ifá's 256 Odù passed orally by babalawos and recognized by UNESCO in 2005; àtúnwá (ancestral rebirth); Ile-Ife as cradle of creation. No firm origin date in the source, so low confidence kept.

trads.d: Chukwu the creator, Ala the earth goddess of morality, personal chi, and the dead reborn among their descendants. The Igbo-Ukwu bronzes date to the 9th century.
trads.an: Odinala with Chukwu as supreme being; Ala and chi not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Nyame the sky god, the earth goddess Asase Yaa and the abosom spirits. The Golden Stool holds the Asante nation's soul.
trads.an: Akan religion with Nyame as supreme being and Asaase Yaa.

trads.d: Fon and Ewe worship of the vodun under the creator pair Mawu-Lisa, with Fa divination. It is the root of Haitian Vodou and is recognized in Benin with a national Vodun holiday.
trads.an: Mawu-Lisa; Vodun in Benin and Togo. The 'official religion of Benin' phrasing was corrected to 'recognized, with a national holiday'.

trads.d: The creator Amma and the Nommo spirits. Masked dances honor the dead, and the Sigui festival is held every 60 years.
trads.an: Dogon religion listed; Amma, Nommo and the 60-year Sigui are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Roog the supreme god, ancestral spirits (pangool) and the Saltigue priests who make yearly predictions.
trads.an: Roog the supreme creator; Saltigue priests and priestesses.

trads.d: Spread by the Bantu expansion: a distant creator (Nzambi, Mulungu, Unkulunkulu), powerful ancestors, and diviner-healers who mediate between them.
trads.an: Bantu religious traditions across Central, East and Southern Africa.

trads.r: Angola, DR Congo, Republic of Congo
trads.d: The Kongo cosmogram maps the cycle of life between the world of the living and that of the ancestors. Nkisi power objects are used for healing and justice.
trads.an: Kongo religion and nkisi.

trads.d: Unkulunkulu, the ancestors (amadlozi), and diviners (izangoma) and herbalists (izinyanga).
trads.an: Zulu religion and amadlozi (ancestors).

trads.d: Mwari the high god, and spirit mediums (svikiro) of lineage and territorial spirits. Great Zimbabwe dates from the 11th to the 15th centuries.
trads.an: Zimbabwean indigenous religion listed; details not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Formed among enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue and recognizable by the mid-18th century. The lwa spirits, grouped in nations such as Rada and Petwo and paired with Catholic saints, are served through drumming, dance and possession under a distant God, Bondye. Many Vodouists fought in the Haitian Revolution; tradition links its start to the Bois Caïman ceremony (1791).
trads.an: Developed in Haiti between the 16th and 19th c., taking recognizable form around the mid-18th c.; Bondye as remote creator; lwa grouped in nations (Rada, Petwo) and linked to saints; possession. Many Vodouists took part in the Haitian Revolution (1791–1801), but the specific Bois Caïman link is not confirmed in the checked source, so it is softened to 'tradition holds'.
kf: the lwa (Papa Legba, Erzulie, Ogou, Damballa, Baron Samedi)

trads.d: Shaped by Haitian refugees and figures such as Marie Laveau.
trads.an: Louisiana Voodoo is a related but distinct tradition.

trads.d: Yoruba Òrìṣà worship reborn in Cuba, with orishas paired with Catholic saints, priestly initiation, Ifá and drum ceremonies.
trads.an: Developed in western Cuba in the late 19th c. from Yoruba religion, Catholicism and Spiritism, so start moved from 1800 to 1870. Oricha paired with saints (Changó with Santa Bárbara, Ochún with Our Lady of Charity); kariocha initiation; Ifá babalawos; batá drumming calls oricha to possess participants; animal sacrifice; Lucumí ritual language; high hundreds of thousands of initiates.

trads.d: A Kongo-derived Cuban religion of the dead and of nature spirits, worked through the nganga (a sacred vessel).
trads.an: A Kongo-derived religion that developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th c., so start moved from 1800 to 1890. The nganga vessel holds the dead (nfumbe); Nsambi is a remote creator; mpungu spirits; branches Mayombe, Monte, Briyumba and Kimbisa.

trads.d: Afro-Brazilian worship of the orixás in houses (terreiros) led by priestesses. The Casa Branca terreiro in Salvador dates from the 1830s.
trads.an: Coalesced in 19th-c. Bahia; Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká (Casa Branca) founded in Salvador in 1830; Ketu, Jeje and Angola nations; most Bahian terreiros led by women.

trads.d: A Brazilian blend of Afro-Brazilian religion, Spiritism, Catholicism and Indigenous spirits. Historians place its formation in 1920s Rio de Janeiro; the tradition dates its founding to a 1908 revelation to Zélio de Moraes.
trads.an: Scholarly sources place Umbanda's formation in 1920s Rio de Janeiro; the tradition's own founding narrative dates it to Zélio de Moraes in 1908. Start moved to 1920, with the 1908 account noted as the tradition's own.

trads.d: Arose in 1930s Jamaica, with Leonard Howell among its first preachers, after Haile Selassie's coronation in 1930, and holds him to be God incarnate or a prophet. It teaches return to Zion (Africa), the Ital diet, dreadlocks and sacramental cannabis, and speaks out against 'Babylon'. It is decentralized (Nyabinghi, Bobo Ashanti, Twelve Tribes) and has about 700,000–1 million adherents.
trads.an: Emerged in 1930s Jamaica after Haile Selassie's 1930 coronation (Leonard Howell); Selassie seen as Jah incarnate or as a prophet; Ital diet; dreadlocks; sacramental cannabis; Babylon and Zion; decentralized (Nyabinghi, Bobo Ashanti, Twelve Tribes); 700,000–1 million adherents; roots in Ethiopianism, Garveyism and Revivalism.

trads.d: Colossal heads, were-jaguar imagery, ball courts and pyramids. These are the roots of Mesoamerican religion.
trads.an: Olmec religion thrived from 1200 to 400 BCE, so start moved from 1500 to 1200 BCE.

trads.d: The ceiba world tree, the 260-day count and the Long Count, the Popol Vuh's successive creations, Xibalba ('place of fright'), and royal bloodletting. Human sacrifice was reserved for exceptional occasions. Maya daykeepers still keep the 260-day calendar.
trads.an: Ceiba world tree; 260-day count and Long Count; Popol Vuh's successive creations; Xibalba; royal bloodletting; human sacrifice only on exceptional occasions; daykeepers still keep the 260-day count.

trads.d: The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the Feathered Serpent temple, where sacrificial victims were buried. It is the model for later Mesoamerican cities.
trads.an: Founded c. 100 BCE, sacked c. 550 CE; the Great Goddess as primary deity, plus the Storm God and Feathered Serpent; sacrificial burials consecrating the Feathered Serpent temple c. 200 CE; the Aztecs later revered the site as the place where the gods were born.

trads.d: Huitzilopochtli, Tlaloc and Quetzalcoatl. Large-scale human sacrifice fed the sun of the fifth and final world age. The dead's destination depended on how they died.
trads.an: Huitzilopochtli, Tlaloc and Quetzalcoatl; Five Suns; afterlife by manner of death (sun, Mictlan, Tlalocan); human-sacrifice estimates vary widely and exceed excavated remains.

trads.d: An oracle center at Chavín de Huántar, where pilgrims entered dark galleries, possibly using San Pedro cactus.
trads.an: Chavín named as a source of Inca religious belief.

trads.d: Pottery and murals show a 'sacrifice ceremony' presided over by priest-warriors, confirmed by excavated tombs.
trads.an: c. 100–800 CE; human sacrifice central in art; Lord of Sipán (found 1987) and Lady of Cao (2005), suggesting priestess-queens.

trads.d: A sacred city whose Gateway of the Sun shows a staff god, ancestral to Viracocha.
trads.an: Founded c. 110 CE (radiocarbon), peaked c. 500–600 and collapsed around 1000, so start moved from 500 to 110. The Gateway of the Sun Staff God is variously identified with Viracocha or Tunuupa; sacrificial dedications at the Akapana; a pilgrimage centre at the 'centre of the universe'.

trads.d: Inti the sun, Viracocha the creator, Pachamama, sacred huacas, royal mummies and capacocha child offerings on mountain peaks. It ended with the fall of Vilcabamba in 1572.
trads.an: Inti (Coricancha, Punchao idol by Pachakuti), Viracocha, Pachamama, huacas, royal mummies consulted as oracles, capacocha child sacrifice; Chavín, Wari and Nazca named as sources.

trads.d: Offerings to Pachamama and the mountain apus continue alongside Catholic saints' festivals, such as Qoyllur Rit'i.
trads.an: Quyllurit'i is a syncretic Andean–Catholic pilgrimage near Cusco (UNESCO 2011), with a Catholic founding story from 1783 and pre-Columbian ties to the Pleiades. Apus and Pachamama offerings are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Burial mounds with exotic grave goods and vast geometric earthworks.
trads.an: Hopewell 100 BCE–500 CE: mounds with exotic grave goods for important people, geometric earthworks (Newark Octagon, a possible lunar observatory) and ceremonial centres. The Adena start date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Platform-mound cities such as Cahokia, the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex's falcon dancers, and chiefs related to the sun.
trads.an: Religion of the Mississippian culture; Green Corn and agricultural cults.

trads.d: Hopi, Zuni and Tewa kachina dances in the kiva and plaza. People emerged from lower worlds, and rain and harmony come through ceremony.
trads.an: Masked kachina dances as prayer (over 500 kachinas), the kiva, and balance for rain. Cliff dwellings date to c. 900–1350, and the source says the religion likely took shape in the late 13th–early 14th c., so start moved from 750 to 1300. The emergence myth is not covered by the checked source.

trads.n: Plains religion and the Sun Dance
trads.d: Wakan Tanka, the 'Great Sacredness' of the Lakota, along with vision quests, the sweat lodge, the sacred pipe and the Sun Dance, which originated with the Shoshone and spread across the Plains. Canada lifted its ban on the full ceremony in 1951.
trads.an: The Sun Dance originated with the Shoshone and spread across Plains nations (pipe, fasting, sometimes piercing; Canada lifted its ban in 1951); Wakan Tanka means 'Great Sacredness' (wording adjusted).

trads.d: Wovoka's vision on 1 January 1889 (after Wodziwob's 1869 movement) promised that dancing in peace would reunite people with the dead and renew the world. Its spread among the Lakota ended in the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890), but it continued quietly, and the Caddo still practise it.
trads.an: Wovoka's vision on 1 January 1889 (preceded by Wodziwob's 1869 movement); taught peace and reunion with the dead; linked to Sitting Bull's death and the Wounded Knee Massacre (29 December 1890). It went underground rather than dying out: the Caddo still practise it, and Lakota danced it in 1973. Status changed from historical (ended 1910) to living.

trads.d: Peyote ceremonies of the Half-Moon and Cross-fire ways, with Christian elements. They spread across Oklahoma's Indian Territory in the late 19th century, and the church was incorporated in 1911 and formally constituted in 1918. It has some 250,000–300,000 members.
trads.an: Arose in late-19th-c. Oklahoma Territory; incorporated 1911 and officially formed 1918; Half-Moon and Cross-fire ways with Christian elements; c. 250,000–300,000 members. An alcohol prohibition is not mentioned in the checked source, so that trait was removed.

trads.d: The Creator and the twins of creation, the Thanksgiving Address and seasonal ceremonies. The Great Law of Peace was founded by the Peacemaker.
trads.an: Sky Woman falls from the sky island and gives birth to twins, the good Sapling (Hah-gweh-di-yu) and destructive Flint, which fits the dual-creation trait; spring thanksgiving dances. The Great Law of Peace, Thanksgiving Address and Green Corn rites are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Handsome Lake's visions (1799) renewed Seneca ceremonies with a moral code against alcohol and witchcraft.
trads.an: Founded 1797/1799 by the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake, with a moral code against drinking and selling land.

trads.d: The Grand Medicine Society, with graded initiations, healing knowledge and sacred birchbark scrolls.
trads.an: Grand Medicine Society of the Anishinaabe.

trads.d: Angakkuit (shamans) placated Sedna, mother of sea animals. Taboos governed hunting and the souls of animals.
trads.an: Angakkuit (men and women); Sedna withholds sea mammals when taboos are broken; animal souls must be respected. Paleo-Eskimo dating is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Zemí images of spirits and ancestors; the cohoba snuff used by behique priests to speak with them.
trads.an: Zemís as deities or ancestral spirits and the objects housing them; creator Yúcahu and fertility goddess Atabey; ancestors' bones kept in zemís and given offerings; medicine people consulted zemís for healing.

trads.d: Shamans heal and negotiate with the spirits of animals and plants, who are also persons. In some regions they use ayahuasca, though how old that practice is remains debated.
trads.an: Shamanic healing through plant spirits is well documented. Ayahuasca's antiquity is debated: suggestive residues from c. 900 CE (Tiwanaku) are not conclusive, the earliest written accounts are 17th–18th century, and some scholars (Gow) argue that mestizo ayahuasca shamanism took shape in colonial missions. The -5000 start for the broader shamanic complex is an estimate. Description reworded.

trads.d: Mestre Irineu's Amazonian Christian religion, with ayahuasca as sacrament and sung hymns.
trads.an: Founded by Raimundo Irineu Serra in Acre in the 1920s–30s; ayahuasca (Daime) as sacrament; hymns (O Cruzeiro); folk Catholic and Kardecist Spiritist elements. Barquinha and UDV are allied ayahuasca churches.

trads.d: Ancestral beings shaped the land in the Dreaming and remain present in country, songlines and ceremony. Songlines can run for thousands of kilometres, and some stories appear to record events over 10,000 years old. Around 900 distinct groups each hold their own law.
trads.an: Ancestral beings shaped the land, with songlines running for thousands of kilometres; some stories match geological events over 10,000 years old; about 900 distinct groups. The unsourced 'oldest continuing traditions' claim was removed.

trads.d: Gods such as Tangaroa and Tāne, Sky Father and Earth Mother (Rangi and Papa), sacred chiefs with mana, tapu (taboo) and marae (sacred courtyards).
trads.an: Sky–earth marriage (Rangi and Papa) and Tangaroa confirmed; other details not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Kū, Kāne, Lono and Kanaloa worshipped at heiau temples, under a strict kapu system abolished in 1819. Practices are revived today.
trads.an: Kū, Kāne, Lono and Kanaloa; heiau temples with offerings and human sacrifice; Makahiki season for Lono with the Kumulipo chant; the kapu system was overthrown in 1819 by Liholiho, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani with the high priest Hewahewa; revival from the 1970s Hawaiian Renaissance.

trads.d: Whakapapa (genealogy) links people to gods, land and ancestors. Tapu and noa govern the sacred and ordinary, and the marae is the center of community.
trads.an: Settlement of New Zealand dated c. 1300 CE, so start moved from 1250 to 1300; Rangi and Papa sky–earth myth.

trads.d: The moai embody deified ancestors. Later, the Birdman (Tangata manu) cult held its competition at Orongo.
trads.an: Moai as deified ancestors facing inland; the later birdman cult of Makemake; declined after conversion to Catholicism. Exact dates and Orongo are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana's healing ministry became a Māori church and political movement.
trads.an: T. W. Rātana's vision on 8 November 1918 began a healing mission; the church was formally established in 1925, its temple opened in 1928, and it allied with Labour (formally 1936). Beliefs centre on the Trinity, the Faithful Angels and Te Māngai. 43,821 adherents in the 2018 census.

trads.d: Te Kooti's Māori faith, drawing on the Hebrew Bible and the Psalms, keeps the 12th day of each month and the Saturday Sabbath.
trads.an: Founded 1868 by Te Kooti, drawing on the Old Testament; 16,000 members (2006 census). The Saturday Sabbath and 12th-of-the-month observance are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Hundreds of local traditions: powerful ancestors, male initiation cults, exchange of wealth with spirits, and sorcery.
trads.an: Ancestor spirits (tamate) and ghost tales; culture heroes Qat, To-Kabinana and Tagaro; cargo cults arose in the 20th c. Initiation cults and exchange with spirits are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Prophetic movements expecting ancestral or messianic delivery of wealth ('cargo'). John Frum, on Tanna, began around 1940.
trads.an: John Frum arose no later than the late 1930s on Tanna; fewer than 500 practitioners in 2022 (Lamakara); John Frum Day on 15 February.

trads.d: Anito spirits and ancestors honored through babaylan (often female) shamans. They survive within folk Catholicism and in Indigenous communities.
trads.an: Anito are ancestor and nature spirits and deities; babaylan (mostly women) enter trance and are possessed in pag-anito séances; devotion transferred to patron saints in folk Catholicism; Bathala as chief Tagalog deity.

trads.d: A Javanese spiritual path blending Hindu–Buddhist, Sufi and Austronesian ideas of inner harmony and union with the divine.
trads.an: Javanism (kebatinan) blends animist, Hindu-Buddhist (from c. 1st c. CE) and Islamic, including Sufi, elements, with Islam adopted around 1500; it seeks inner harmony and union through meditation, fasting and tapa. Recognized in 1973 as a 'belief in One God', not a religion.

trads.d: The 'way of the ancestors', famous for grand funerals with water buffalo sacrifice, cliff graves and tau tau effigies.
trads.an: Aluk To Dolo, 'the way of the ancestors', is a polytheistic animism that is also law and custom; Puang Matua is the creator. Funerals slaughter water buffalo for the journey to Puya; cliff tombs and tau tau effigies. Legalized in 1969 as a sect of Agama Hindu Dharma; today a small minority after Dutch missions from the 1920s.

trads.d: Zanahary the creator and the razana (ancestors). In famadihana, families rewrap and dance with the bones of the dead. Fady taboos regulate daily life.
trads.an: Famadihana: every five to seven years families exhume and rewrap ancestors and dance with them; possibly only since the 17th c. in its present form, adapting older Austronesian double-funeral customs. Zanahary and fady are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Deism is belief in a creator known through reason and nature rather than revelation (Herbert of Cherbury, 1624). It influenced Voltaire, Paine and Jefferson.
trads.an: Herbert of Cherbury's De Veritate (1624) was the first major English statement. Toland's Christianity Not Mysterious (1696); Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), the 'Deist's Bible'; Voltaire; Paine's Age of Reason (1793–94). Jefferson held Deistic principles but called himself a Unitarian.
kt: Christianity as Old as the Creation

trads.d: A non-religious life stance of reason, ethics and human flourishing, set out in the Humanist Manifesto (1933). It is part of the roughly 24% of people who are religiously unaffiliated.
trads.an: Humanist Manifesto I (1933), whose signers called themselves religious humanists; Manifesto II (1973, Kurtz and Wilson); A Secular Humanist Declaration (1980); Amsterdam Declaration (1952, revised 2002 and 2022). Paul Kurtz is considered the founder of the American secular humanist movement.

trads.d: Felix Adler's 'deed, not creed' congregations, which put ethics in place of theology.
trads.an: Felix Adler's 1876 sermon led to the New York Society for Ethical Culture, founded 1877 (start moved from 1876). Motto 'deed before creed'; American Ethical Union 1893; British societies from 1886 (Stanton Coit).

trads.d: Anton LaVey's atheistic philosophy uses Satan as a symbol of individualism and self-assertion. It does not worship any deity.
trads.an: Church of Satan founded Walpurgisnacht 1966 in San Francisco; Satan as a symbol, LaVey an atheist; Satanic Bible 1969.

trads.d: A non-theistic activist religion with Seven Tenets of compassion, reason and bodily autonomy, known for church–state cases.
trads.an: Founded in 2013.

trads.d: L. Ron Hubbard's movement teaches that humans are immortal thetans who free themselves through 'auditing'. Its upper levels are confidential.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: L. Ron Hubbard (1911–1986); Church founded 1954.
kt: Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health

trads.d: Claude Vorilhon (Raël) taught that extraterrestrial Elohim created humanity in laboratories.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Claude Vorilhon (born 1946).
kt: The Book Which Tells the Truth (Intelligent Design)

trads.d: Paul Twitchell's 'religion of the Light and Sound of God', adapted from Sant Mat.
trads.an: Founder confirmed: Paul Twitchell (1908–1971).

trads.d: Followers of Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), who rejected strict predestination in favor of free will and resisted grace. Arminian theology later shaped Methodism.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Philipp Spener's movement for heartfelt personal devotion, small Bible-study circles and holy living. It fed Moravian, Methodist and evangelical revivals.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Anabaptist-Pietist 'Dunkers' from Schwarzenau who baptize by triple immersion, keep a love feast with foot-washing and witness for peace.
trads.an: Founded 1708 at Schwarzenau by Alexander Mack and seven others; believer's baptism by trine immersion; love feast with foot washing; one of the three historic peace churches; about 600,000 members worldwide (2020).

trads.d: The first Anabaptist circle around Conrad Grebel (c. 1498–1526) in Zurich, whose adult baptisms of January 1525 began the movement.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Founded by Richard Allen and other Black Methodists in Philadelphia after discrimination in white churches. It is the oldest independent Black denomination in the US.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Lay-led assemblies without clergy that 'break bread' weekly. J. N. Darby's dispensationalism (a rapture before the end-times) spread widely through them.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.
kt: Synopsis of the Books of the Bible (Darby)

trads.d: Formed when Baptists in the South split from northern Baptists over slavery (1845). It later became America's largest Protestant body and apologized for its racist origins in 1995.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: The Oxford Movement (1833) revived Catholic liturgy, sacramental theology and religious orders within Anglicanism.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: A leading Holiness denomination teaching entire sanctification.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.
kt: Manual of the Church of the Nazarene

trads.d: The largest African-American Pentecostal church, organized by Charles Harrison Mason after Azusa Street.
trads.an: C. H. Mason's church, interracial before the 1920s (founded 1907 per the Christianity timeline).

trads.d: Founded at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914. Today one of the largest Pentecostal fellowships worldwide.
trads.an: General Council of the Assemblies of God created in Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914.

trads.d: Pentecostals who reject the Trinity and baptize 'in Jesus' name only', from the 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting onward.
trads.an: The Oneness issue emerged at a 1913 camp meeting, and Oneness churches withdrew from the Assemblies of God in 1916.

trads.d: Founded by the evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson (1890–1944) at Angelus Temple in Los Angeles.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: A 1925 union of Methodists, most Presbyterians and Congregationalists. It is Canada's largest Protestant church.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: A 1957 merger of Congregational Christian and Evangelical and Reformed churches. It is theologically liberal.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: A 1947 union of Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches, joining episcopal and Protestant traditions.
trads.an: Formed 27 September 1947 in Madras from Anglican, South India United (Congregational, Presbyterian, Reformed) and Methodist churches; combines episcopal, presbyterian and congregational elements; about 4.5–5 million members.

trads.d: Chuck Smith's Costa Mesa church that welcomed the 'Jesus People' hippie converts and pioneered contemporary worship.
trads.an: Founded 1965 by Chuck Smith in Costa Mesa; a hub of the Jesus movement and contemporary Christian music; about 1,800 churches (2022) plus a 1,000-church breakaway network.

trads.d: John Wimber's 'third wave' charismatic movement of signs and wonders within evangelicalism.
trads.an: John Wimber, a Calvary Chapel pastor, parted ways in 1982 over spiritual manifestations and led what became the Association of Vineyard Churches.

trads.n: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God
trads.d: Edir Macedo's neo-Pentecostal church, known for prosperity teaching and exorcism.
trads.an: Founded 1977 in Rio de Janeiro by Edir Macedo; prosperity theology, 10% tithing and exorcism ('deliverance'); headquarters at the Temple of Solomon in São Paulo (2014); estimates of 3–8 million members worldwide; controversies and bans in some countries.

trads.d: Founded by Josiah Akindayomi out of the Cherubim and Seraphim milieu. It became a Pentecostal megachurch network known for its Redemption Camp.
trads.an: About 14,000 churches and 5 million members in Africa (2020); founding year not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Samuel Oschoffa's Aladura-type church of visions, healing and white garments, worshipping barefoot.
trads.an: Founded 29 September 1947 at Porto-Novo by Samuel Oshoffa after a revelation; white garments worn barefoot; tobacco, alcohol and pork forbidden; nearly half a million followers in Benin (2001); strongest in Nigeria.

trads.d: The Liberian prophet William Wadé Harris baptized over 100,000 people along the Ivory Coast in 1913–15, and his followers formed an independent church.
trads.an: Harris began his mission on 27 July 1913 and baptized over 100,000 converts in about 18 months (1913–14) along the Ivory Coast, burning fetishes and tolerating polygamy. Many converts later joined Catholic and Methodist churches, while others formed independent Harrist churches.

trads.d: Isaiah Shembe's Zulu church, which blends Christianity with Zulu dance, a Saturday Sabbath and pilgrimage to Ekuphakameni.
trads.an: Isaiah Shembe named as founder; year not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: A Luo African Catholic church of exorcism and healing, whose founder Simeo Ondeto is venerated as a black Messiah.
trads.an: Split from the Catholic Church in Nyanza in 1963 (roots from 1938–40), led by Simeo Ondetto and Mama Maria. Gaudencia Aoko was a prophet, not a founder. Followers hold Ondetto to be the returned Son of God ('Black Messiah'); healing and exorcism; roughly 3 million members (2004).

trads.n: Brotherhood of the Cross and Star
trads.d: Olumba Olumba Obu (1918–2003), proclaimed by followers as the Holy Spirit incarnate, preached love and vegetarianism from Calabar.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: A Chinese independent Pentecostal church (Beijing, 1917) that is Oneness, keeps a Saturday Sabbath and practises foot-washing.

trads.d: Watchman Nee's 'one city, one church' assemblies, later led by Witness Lee.
trads.an: Watchman Nee began meeting outside denominations in 1922 and taught 'one church per city' from 1926; Witness Lee led the worldwide spread; Living Stream Ministry; an estimated 0.5–2 million members, mostly in China.

trads.d: A nationalist break from Rome led by Gregorio Aglipay during the Philippine Revolution, now in communion with the Anglicans.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: A reformed Saint Thomas Christian church that keeps its Syriac liturgy with Protestant theology.
trads.an: Abraham Malpan's reforms from the 1830s; reformist bishops excommunicated in 1875, and the 1889 court verdict made the Mar Thoma Church independent; reformed West Syriac liturgy in Malayalam; in communion with Anglicans (and Old Catholics since 2024); about 1 million members.

trads.d: Separated from the Ethiopian Church after Eritrean independence (autocephaly 1993–94).
trads.an: Autocephalous after Eritrean independence (1993), recognized by the Coptic Church in 1994; about 3 million members; Patriarch Antonios was deposed in 2006, reportedly under government pressure.

trads.d: Orthodox who rejected the 1924 switch to the Revised Julian calendar.
trads.an: Formed after the Churches of Greece and Romania adopted the Revised Julian calendar in 1924 (Bulgaria in 1968); several Greek factions, one Romanian church; estimates of 0.5–0.8 million in Greece and about 1 million in Romania.

trads.d: Polish-American parishes that broke from Rome over control of parish property and ethnic leadership.
trads.an: Founded March 1897 in Scranton by Franciszek Hodur over the hierarchy's neglect of Polish immigrants and property disputes; married clergy since 1921; expelled from the Utrecht Union in 2003 over women's ordination; about 30,000 members.

trads.d: An Old Catholic offshoot led by Theosophists, keeping Catholic sacraments and teaching reincarnation and karma.
trads.an: Wedgwood (consecrated 1916) and Leadbeater combined Catholic sacraments with Theosophy (The Science of the Sacraments). Reincarnation and karma are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: A sacramental movement for religious renewal founded in 1922 by Lutheran ministers led by Friedrich Rittelmeyer, inspired by Rudolf Steiner.
trads.an: Founded in Germany in 1922 by Lutheran ministers led by Friedrich Rittelmeyer, inspired by Steiner's Christology (the source does not say Steiner co-founded it); men and women ordained; about 30,000–35,000 members in 200 congregations. Description reworded.

trads.d: John Humphrey Noyes's perfectionist commune, practising shared property and 'complex marriage'.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: George Rapp's celibate, communal Pietists, who awaited Christ's imminent return.
trads.an: George Rapp's Separatists organized in 1805 at Harmony, Pennsylvania; community of goods; celibacy from c. 1807–08; expected Christ's imminent return; moved to New Harmony and Economy; dissolved in 1905 with three members left.

trads.d: Eberhard Arnold's Christian communities, which share all goods in the Anabaptist tradition.
trads.an: Founded 1920 by Eberhard and Emmy Arnold at Sannerz, Germany; Anabaptist, pacifist; full community of goods; 24 communities and about 3,000 members (2024).

trads.d: An Adventist offshoot from the Davidians (1930s). Its Waco compound under David Koresh ended in a deadly 1993 siege and fire. Small groups continue.
trads.an: Victor Houteff's Davidian Seventh-day Adventists near Waco; Benjamin Roden's Branch formed in 1955; Vernon Howell (David Koresh) took control in 1987. The February 1993 ATF raid and 51-day siege ended on 19 April 1993 with fires killing about 76 (cause disputed). Small successor groups remain.

trads.d: Herbert W. Armstrong's Sabbath-keeping, festival-observing church. After his death it embraced mainstream evangelicalism (renamed Grace Communion International, 2009), and splinters kept his teachings.
trads.an: Founded as the Radio Church of God in 1934 by Herbert W. Armstrong: Saturday Sabbath, annual holy days, food laws, three tithes, non-trinitarian, British Israelism. Reforms from 1988 brought it into mainstream evangelicalism, and it was renamed Grace Communion International in 2009; splinter groups kept Armstrong's teachings.

trads.d: A Baloch Mahdist minority that replaces salat with dhikr and the Mecca pilgrimage with Koh-e-Murad. Its link to the Mahdavia is disputed.
trads.an: A Mahdist minority of Balochistan's Makran coast, usually dated to the late 16th c. (Nur Pak c. 1569–70), so start moved from 1550 to 1570. Zikr replaces the five salat and Koh-e-Murad replaces the Hajj; about 600,000–800,000 adherents. The link to the Mahdavia is disputed, so the Mahdavia is now an influence rather than the parent.

trads.d: An Ahmadiyya branch that sees Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as a reformer (mujaddid) rather than a prophet.
trads.an: Split in 1914 under Maulana Muhammad Ali after Nur-ud-Din's death; sees Ghulam Ahmad as mujaddid and Messiah but not a prophet in the technical sense; led by an Amir with no caliph; up to 30,000 worldwide.

trads.d: Clarence 13X (1922–1969) taught that the Black man is God. It became influential in hip-hop.

trads.d: Muhammad Ilyas's lay missionary movement, which calls Muslims to deeper practice.
trads.an: Founded 1926 by Muhammad Ilyas in Mewat; a Deobandi lay missionary movement of self-funded preaching tours; centres at Raiwind and Nizamuddin; Pew estimates 12–80 million adherents; split into two factions since 2016.

trads.d: A South Asian Salafi movement that rejects following a single law school in favor of hadith.
trads.an: A mid-19th-c. North Indian reform movement (Syed Nazeer Husain, Siddiq Hasan Khan) that rejects taqlid of the four schools; emerged as a distinct group c. 1864, so start moved from 1860 to 1864; often equated with Salafism.

trads.d: Muslims who accept the Qur'an alone and reject hadith as authority.
trads.an: The Qur'an as the sole source with hadith not binding; decentralized; modern forms from the 19th–20th c. in British India and Egypt (Syed Ahmad Khan, Abdullah Chakralawi, Ghulam Ahmed Perwez, Rashad Khalifa).

trads.d: Schneur Zalman of Liadi's intellectual Hasidism, which in the 20th century became a worldwide outreach movement.
trads.an: Founded 1775 at Liozno by Shneur Zalman of Liadi (Tanya, 1797); named for Lyubavichi; moved to Brooklyn in 1940; Menachem Mendel Schneerson (1951–1994) expanded it; over 6,500 emissary families; about 90,000–95,000 members.

trads.d: Opponents of Hasidism led by the Vilna Gaon, who stressed rigorous Talmud study in yeshivas.
trads.an: The anti-Hasidic movement centred on Vilna; the first excommunications came in 1772 with the Vilna Gaon's polemical letters; Chaim of Volozhin pioneered the modern yeshiva; heirs known as Litvishe or Yeshivish.

trads.d: Israel Salanter's ethical movement, which cultivated character through introspection and moral study.
trads.an: Israel Salanter (1810–1883) founded the movement among Lithuanian Orthodox Jews; his Kovno Musar yeshiva dates to c. 1848, so start moved from 1840 to 1848. It stressed ethical self-work, business ethics and texts such as Mesillat Yesharim.

trads.d: Torah observance combined with secular learning (Torah im Derech Eretz). Its founders include Samson Raphael Hirsch and Azriel Hildesheimer (1820–1899).
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Strictly Orthodox communities that resist modern secular culture, encompassing Hasidic and Lithuanian streams.
trads.an: A strictly Orthodox response to emancipation and the Haskalah. Most historians date modern Haredi Judaism to the early 20th c., so start moved from 1850 to 1900. Hasidic, Lithuanian and (from the 1980s) Sephardic streams; about 2.1 million worldwide (2020), about 14% of world Jewry.

trads.d: Orthodox Zionism (the Mizrachi movement, 1902) sees the return to Israel as part of redemption.
trads.an: Mizrachi founded in Vilna in 1902 with the slogan 'the people of Israel in the land of Israel according to the Torah of Israel'; Abraham Isaac Kook (Chief Rabbi from 1924) saw Zionism as part of redemption; Hesder yeshivas.

trads.d: Hungary's moderate reformist stream, formed after the 1868–69 Jewish Congress.
trads.an: Formed when the 1868–69 Hungarian Jewish Congress split Neologs from the Orthodox and Status Quo; shaped by Frankel's Positive-Historical school; today Hungary's majority stream (MAZSIHISZ).

trads.d: Kang Youwei and Chen Huanzhang's effort to make Confucianism a congregational religion.
trads.an: Proposed by Kang Youwei and founded by Chen Huanzhang in 1912, with 132 branches before 1920s anti-religious campaigns dissolved it on the mainland. It continues through Hong Kong's Confucian Academy and an Indonesian supreme council.

trads.d: Yoshida Kanetomo's 'primal' Shintō claiming independence from Buddhism. It controlled shrine ranks for centuries.
trads.an: Created by Yoshida Kanetomo (1435–1511) in the Sengoku period as 'One-and-only Shintō', reversing honji suijaku so that Buddhist deities are manifestations of kami; the 1665 regulations made the Yoshida supervisors of lesser shrines until the late Edo period.

trads.d: Motoori Norinaga and Hirata Atsutane's 'national learning', which sought a pure Shintō before Chinese and Buddhist influence.
trads.an: An Edo-period 'national learning' turning from Chinese, Confucian and Buddhist texts to early Japanese classics, traditionally founded by Kada no Azumamaro (1669–1736), with Kamo no Mabuchi, Motoori Norinaga and Hirata Atsutane; it fed State Shinto and sonnō jōi. Start moved from 1760 to 1700.

trads.an: Followers regard Kang Jeungsan (d. 1909) as the incarnation of Sangje, the Supreme God; an umbrella for more than 100 movements, including Bocheon-gyo (claimed about 6 million in the 1920s) and Jeung San Do (1974). The 1901 revelation date is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Worship of Dangun, the mythic founder of Korea, revived during Japanese rule.
trads.an: Founded in Seoul in 1909 by Na Cheol (1864–1916) as Dangunism, renamed a year later; Dangun is seen as the human manifestation of a trinitarian God, Haneullim; a focus of the independence movement in Manchuria; about 400,000 followers in the 1910s but fewer than 10,000 in the 1995 census.

trads.d: The largest Jeungsanist order.
trads.an: Founded in 1969 by Park Wudang, successor of Jo Jeongsan's Mugeukdo (1925); apparently the largest Jeungsanist group; split after Park's death in 1996.

trads.d: Vietnamese worship of mother goddesses with hầu đồng mediumship rituals, in which mediums embody the deities while staying in control. Inscribed by UNESCO in 2016.
trads.an: Established in the 16th c., so start moved from 1500 to 1550; inscribed by UNESCO in December 2016. In the hầu bóng ceremony the medium stays in control and deities do not enter the body, so the possession trait was removed and the description reworded.

trads.d: Dinka, Nuer and Maasai traditions of a sky creator (Nhialic, Kwoth, Enkai), cattle sacrifice and spirit-powers.
trads.an: Dinka Nhialic, the distant sky and rain creator (Jaak/Juong among the Nuer and Shilluk); cattle sacrifice with prayer; jok ancestral spirits and patron powers.

trads.d: Enkai (Ngai), the dual-natured god, with the laibon (ritual expert) and age-set initiations.
trads.an: Monotheistic: Enkai or Engai, whose dual nature is Engai Narok (Black God, benevolent) and Engai Na-nyokie (Red God, vengeful). The laibon provides healing, divination and prophecy. Age-sets were adopted from Cushitic neighbours; circumcision; Eunoto marks the move from warrior to junior elder. No arrival date given (the 1500 start is an estimate).

trads.d: Ngai on Mount Kenya, ancestral spirits and sacred fig trees.
trads.an: Ngai, the distant High God linked to Mount Kenya, appears in thunder, rainbows and fig trees. Sacrifice under the mugumo (fig) or mũkũyũ (sycamore). Ancestors, led by Gĩkũyũ and Mũmbi, are venerated. Kenyatta's Facing Mount Kenya (1938) is a key early account. Most Kikuyu are now Christian.

trads.d: Initiation religion of the Punu, Mitsogo and Fang of Gabon, said to come from Pygmy groups, using the iboga root. It honours ancestors and is often blended with Catholicism.
trads.an: Practised by the Punu, Mitsogo and Fang of Gabon and said to originate among Pygmy (Mbenge) groups; iboga initiation is the crucial rite; often syncretized with Catholicism; honors ancestors. No founding date: iboga has been used 'for hundreds of years', so start moved to 1600 at low confidence.

trads.d: The Oromo faith in one supreme creator, Waaqa, with Qaalluu priests and the Gadaa age-grade system. The Irreecha thanksgiving at Lake Hora Harsedi now draws millions.
trads.an: Waaqa is the supreme creator (the source does not call him a sky god, so that trait was removed); Qaalluu priests uphold Gadaa; the Irreecha thanksgiving at Lake Hora Harsedi draws millions. Active practitioners are estimated at c. 1.1 million, with other estimates up to 5 million.

trads.d: Worship of Amun-like and local deities, ancestors and sacred places among the Amazigh before Christianity and Islam.
trads.an: Amun with his oracle at Siwa, Tanit, Gurzil (temple at Ghirza used into the 6th c.), Ifri; dream incubation at ancestral tombs (Herodotus); persisted among tribes into the 7th c. and faded after the Arab conquest.

trads.d: Achamán the sky god and mummification of the dead. It ended with the Castilian conquest.
trads.an: Guanches mummified their dead, unlike most mainland Berbers. Achamán is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: K. O. K. Onyioha's pan-African 'Godian Religion' reinterpreting traditional faith.
trads.an: Godianism founded 1948.

trads.d: Kwabena Damuah's reformed African traditional religion.
trads.an: Vincent Kwabena Damuah, a Catholic priest from 1957 who sat on the PNDC in 1982, left the church and founded the Afrikania Mission in December 1982 to reform and promote African traditional religion alongside Pan-Africanism. Successors: Kofi Ameve, then Atsu Kove.

trads.d: Afro-Surinamese spirit religion of possession by winti spirits.
trads.an: Blends Akan, Fon and Kongo beliefs brought by enslaved Africans; winti spirits created by the supreme Anana in earth, water, forest and sky pantheons; possession; outlawed from 1874 until 1971.

trads.d: Caribbean healing and spiritual power practices of West African origin, long criminalized under colonial law.

trads.d: Kongo-derived ancestor rites brought by indentured Central Africans after emancipation.
trads.an: 19th-c. Jamaica (St Thomas), from Kongo-region indentured labourers after abolition; spirit possession for healing; its drumming shaped Nyabinghi and reggae.

trads.d: An Afro-Christian movement born in the Great Revival of 1860–61.
trads.an: Revivalism split into Zion ('60 Order', more Christian) and Pocomania ('61 Order', more Myal). The order names point to the 1860–61 Great Revival, but Wikipedia dates the 'Great Myal Revival' to 1858–59. Leaders are titled Shepherd, Captain and Mother; worship includes trance, possession, prophecy and ritual dance.
kf: spirits of the heavens and the earth

trads.d: A Shouter Baptist faith, banned in Trinidad from 1917 to 1951.
trads.an: In Trinidad it traces to Merikins (formerly enslaved Americans who fought for Britain in 1812) settled c. 1815–16, so start moved from 1850 to 1816. Banned by the Shouter Prohibition Ordinance 1917–1951; Liberation Day (30 March) a public holiday since 1996; invoking the Holy Spirit; coloured gowns and headties.

trads.d: Yoruba orisha worship, with Shango prominent, among Trinidadians.

trads.d: Afro-Brazilian practice that grew alongside Umbanda, taking up what Umbanda rejected. It centres on the Exus and Pombagiras ('spirits of the left'), with rituals at crossroads.
trads.an: Grew out of the broader Macumba complex as the 'sibling' of Umbanda (1920s Rio), taking what Umbanda rejected; centred on Exus and Pombagiras ('spirits of the left'), with rituals at crossroads, sometimes involving animal sacrifice; grew strongly from the 1970s. Start moved from 1950 to 1930 and description reworded.

trads.d: Afro-Brazilian orixá worship of southern Brazil.
trads.an: Wikipedia credits Custódio Joaquim de Almeida ('the Prince', d. 1935) in Porto Alegre in the late 19th or early 20th century, while other scholarship traces Batuque houses earlier in the 19th century; the 1850 start is uncertain. Orixá worship with possession; later spread to Uruguay, Argentina and Chile.

trads.d: Afro-Brazilian worship of vodun and encantados, founded in São Luís's Casa das Minas.
trads.an: Mainly practised in Maranhão, Piauí, Pará and the Amazon; Casa das Minas in São Luís was founded in the 1840s; Fon (Jeje) vodun and encantados; songs in Ewe-Fon.

trads.d: A men's initiatory society from the Ekpe of the Cross River region.
trads.an: A Cuban men's initiatory fraternity derived from the Ékpè society of the Cross River region; first lodge formed in Regla in 1836; controlled much of Cuban port labour from the 1870s to 1942.
