trads.d: Venezuelan devotion to the nature goddess María Lionza and a court of spirits.
trads.an: Goddess of nature, love and harmony, centred on Sorte Mountain (pilgrimage every 12 October); spirit courts (Indigenous, African, Viking, Liberator) including Guaicaipuro, Negro Felipe and Bolívar; mediums lead devotees into trance. A 20th-c. blend; the Sorte rituals are dated to the early 1920s, so start moved from 1900 to 1920.

trads.d: Cocijo the rain god and royal ancestors at Monte Albán.
trads.an: Polytheistic, with fertility and agriculture deities; Cocijo is the rain god (like Tlaloc); deified rulers; the elite believed they descended from cloud-people and returned to the clouds at death. Monte Albán's capital period begins c. 700–500 BC. Spanish conquest 1521. Ancestor worship is implied but not stated explicitly.

trads.d: Sué the sun and Chía the moon, and offerings of gold (the origin of the El Dorado legend) at Lake Guatavita.
trads.an: Sué (sun) and Chía (moon), Bochica, and Chibchacum (rain, offered gold); gold and emerald offerings at sacred lakes such as Guatavita fed the El Dorado legend. The last public ceremony was on 27 December 1563 at Ubaque, so end moved from 1600 to 1563.

trads.d: Ngünechen the creator and machi healers, mostly women, who climb the rewe pole in trance. The ngillatun community prayer includes offerings and animal sacrifice.
trads.an: The machi (mostly women) heals and divines, climbing the rewe pole (an axis mundi) in trance flight; the ngillatun community prayer includes offerings and animal sacrifice. The name Ngünechen for the main deity is attested from the 19th c. In 2001, 8% followed traditional religion only. Sacrifice and world-axis traits added.

trads.d: Ñanderuvusu the creator and migrations toward the 'Land without Evil'.
trads.an: The Paraguayan Guarani myth cycle (Tupã, Arasy, Rupave and Sypave, Tau and Kerana) was reshaped by 16th-century Jesuit missions. The 'Land without Evil' migrations and Ñanderuvusu come from Mbyá and Apapocuva ethnography (Nimuendajú) and were not confirmed by the fetched source. Dates are estimates; the myths were unwritten until modern times.

trads.d: Hózhó (beauty, harmony), Holy People and sandpainting healing chantways.
trads.an: Diné Bahaneʼ describes emergence through four worlds, the Holy People (Diyin Dineʼé) who gave the ceremonies, Changing Woman and the Hero Twins, and chantways such as the Night Chant. Hózhó, the Blessingway, sandpainting and the c. 1400 arrival are standard in the ethnographic literature but were not confirmed by the fetched source.
kf: Hero Twins (Monster Slayer, Born for Water)

trads.d: Guardian spirits, totem poles, winter ceremonies and the potlatch gift feast, which Canada banned from 1885 to 1951.
trads.an: The potlatch gift feast (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw, Coast Salish and others) honors the supernatural and ancestral lineages; secret-society dances (hamatsa); banned in Canada from 1884/85 until 1951. Guardian spirits and totem poles are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Secret societies and dances impersonating spirits.
trads.an: Patwin, Maidu, Pomo, Miwok, Ohlone, Esselen, Salinan and northern Yokuts of Northern and Central California. All men joined ceremonial societies that met in underground dance rooms; masked dancers impersonated spirits such as the red-beaked healer Kuksu. Pre-contact; no origin date given (the 500 CE start is an estimate).

trads.d: The Green Corn ceremony, a sacred fire and a medicine tradition.
trads.an: Sacred fire is central (Nabokov: 'the medium of transformation'); medicine people use plant remedies guided by plant spirits; Unetlanvhi the Creator; Selu and Kanáti. The Green Corn ceremony is not covered by this source, though it is widely documented elsewhere for Southeastern peoples.

trads.d: Smohalla's prophetic revival of the Washani religion and Washat dance from about 1850, which urged a return to ancestral ways under God and Mother Earth.
trads.an: Smohalla (c. 1815–1895), a Wanapum prophet, revived the Washani religion and Washat dance from about 1850, urging a return to ancestral ways under God and Mother Earth. The source does not mention his rejection of farming, so the description was reworded.

trads.d: The peyote pilgrimage to Wirikuta and rites for the deer, maize and rain.
trads.an: Annual peyote (hikuri) pilgrimage to Wirikuta; Corn, Blue Deer and Peyote descend from the Sun God; Rain Goddess; shamanic practice largely survived colonial pressure.

trads.d: Mestre Gabriel's (1922–1971) ayahuasca church.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.an: Named as an allied ayahuasca church of Santo Daime; date from standard references.

trads.d: Day of the Dead, saint fiestas and cofradías, blending Catholic and Indigenous rites.
trads.an: Day of the Dead blends Mesoamerican rites with Catholic All Saints and All Souls; home ofrendas; inscribed by UNESCO in 2008. Scholars debate the balance of the two sources.

trads.d: A folk-saint cult of 'Holy Death', first reported in 1940s Mexico City and public since Enriqueta Romero opened a street shrine in 2001. It is condemned by the Catholic Church and has an estimated 12 million devotees.
trads.an: First reported by anthropologists in 1940s Mexico City (Tepito); went public when Enriqueta Romero opened a street shrine in 2001; condemned by the Catholic Church and denounced by Pope Francis in 2016; about 12 million devotees (2016–17). Scholars debate any link to the Aztec death goddess Mictēcacihuātl. Description updated.

trads.d: The war god 'Oro, marae temples and the Arioi society of performers.
trads.an: ʻOro, god of war (and of the arts in peacetime); Taputapuatea marae on Raiatea is his mythical birthplace; the Arioi society traced its founding to him; human sacrifice was witnessed by Cook in 1777. The 1815 end date (Pōmare II's conversion and victory) was not confirmed by this source.

trads.d: The sacred Tu'i Tonga paramount chiefs and gods of the sky and underworld (Pulotu).
trads.an: The Tuʻi Tonga line began in the 10th century with the semi-divine ʻAhoʻeitu; Tāufaʻāhau defeated Laufilitonga in 1826; the last Tuʻi Tonga died in 1865 and the title was abolished in 1875. The 1830 end (Christian conversion) and Pulotu are standard but not covered by this source.

trads.d: The snake god Degei, ancestor gods and chiefly mana.
trads.an: Fijian myth of the serpent Ndengei (Degei), who hatches two children from eggs.

trads.d: Te Ua Haumēne's Māori prophetic faith (from 1862), which blended Old Testament morality with Māori spirituality during the New Zealand Wars. Much of it passed into Ringatū.
trads.an: Te Ua Haumēne's revelation in September 1862; flourished 1863–1874 amid the New Zealand Wars; blended Old Testament morality with Māori spirituality, observed the Sabbath and held rites at the niu pole; 609 adherents in 2006. Elements were absorbed into Ringatū (1868). Sabbath trait and Ringatū link added.

trads.d: Paliau Maloat's movement for church and social reform.
trads.an: Paliau Maloat (c. 1907–1991) returned to Manus in 1946 preaching self-reliance and equality, and founded the Baluan United Christian Church. The 'Noise' cargo-cult outbreak of 1946–47, which he repudiated, was followed by a second in 1953–54. He founded the millenarian Wind Nation in the 1980s. Studied by Mead and Schwartz.

trads.d: The Dayak faith of Ranying Hatalla, with the Panaturan scripture and the Tiwah second funeral. It was grouped under Hinduism from 1980 and recognized as an indigenous belief in 2017.
trads.an: Dayak folk religion of Central and South Kalimantan with the Panaturan scripture; the 30-day Tiwah second funeral with animal sacrifice. Grouped under Hindu Dharma from 1980 and recognized as an indigenous belief (Aliran Kepercayaan) since November 2017; about 330,000 adherents. Description updated.

trads.d: Ancestor spirits, megalithic tombs and the Pasola ritual battle.
trads.an: Ancestral faith of Sumba (and parts of Flores) with an eternal afterlife in Prai Marapu; megalithic tombs are still built; about 100,000 followers in 2023, down from about 200,000 in 2000; not an official religion, though a 2017 court ruling opened ID recognition. Pasola is not covered by this source.

trads.d: Batak worship of Debata Mulajadi Nabolon, formalized by Raja Mulia Naipospos.
trads.an: Malim worship Mula Jadi Na Bolon as the one God and trace their heritage to Sisingamangaraja XII. Raja Mulia Naipospos was an early leader. It arose in Toba lands in the late 19th to early 20th century (an 1870 start is approximate), with its main centre at Huta Tinggi near Laguboti.

trads.d: Sundanese ancestral faith of the Baduy people.
trads.an: Sang Hyang Kersa (Batara Tunggal) is the highest power, with Hindu gods as subordinates. Practised by the Baduy of Kanekes in Banten and other Sundanese; called Jatisunda in the Carita Parahyangan; claims pre-Hindu antiquity and absorbed Hindu and some Islamic elements. About 50,000 adherents.

trads.d: Muhammad Subuh's latihan spiritual exercise, organized from 1947.
trads.an: Subud was founded in the 1920s by Muhammad Subuh, within Javanese kebatinan.

trads.d: Groups that venerate José Rizal as a Filipino Christ.
trads.an: Rizalistas venerate José Rizal as God, Christ reincarnate or a spiritual guide; many believe he is still alive; groups include Iglesia ng Watawat ng Lahi and the Philippine Benevolent Missionaries Association; Colorums prevalent in the 1920s–30s. No founding dates in the checked source.

trads.d: The sacred-grove (sarna) faith of the Munda, Santal, Ho and Oraon peoples, with pahan priests and deities such as Singbonga and Marang Buru. About 5 million people declared it in the 2011 census.
trads.an: Followed by Santal, Oraon, Ho and Munda; communal offerings twice a year in sacred groves (sarna) led by pahan priests; deities Gram Deota, Marang Buru, Singbonga and the earth mother Chalapachho Devi ('Dharmes' is not in the source, so removed); 4,957,467 followers in the 2011 census; activists seek a separate census code.

trads.d: The 'Sun–Moon' faith of the Adi and Tani peoples, organized as a religion from 1986.
trads.an: A revivalist movement among the Adi and other Tani peoples venerating Donyi (Mother Sun) and Polo (Father Moon); the revival began after a 1968 meeting and was formalized in 1986 (Donyi-Polo Yelam Kebang) by Talom Rukbo; about 363,000 followers in 2011. Scholars see the organized form as a 20th-c. development, so it is now dated 1968 as a modern revival of older Tani traditions.

trads.d: The Meitei religion of the creator Sanamahi and Lainingthou deities, revived since the 1930s.
trads.an: Ethnic polytheism of the Meitei named after Lainingthou Sanamahi; amaiba and amaibi priests under the Maru Loishang; Lai Haraoba festival with possessed priestesses; revival from 1930 (Apokpa Marup); 222,422 adherents in 2011.

trads.d: The oral scripture (Mundhum) and ancestor rites of the Kirati peoples.
trads.an: Followed by Rai, Limbu, Yakkha, Sunuwar and others; the oral Mundhum serves as myth, ritual and customary law; shamanism and ancestor and nature worship; nakchhong and phedangma priests; 924,204 adherents (3.17%) in Nepal's 2021 census.

trads.d: The Bodo worship of Bathou (Bwrai), represented by the sacred siju plant.
trads.an: Bodo folk religion of the unseen supreme deity Bathoubwrai, embodied in the sijou plant at the household altar; Mainao protects the rice fields; Kherai festival; douri and doudini priests, with a revival by the All Bathou Religious Union (1992).

trads.d: The Khasi faith in one God (U Blei), revived by the Seng Khasi in 1899.
trads.an: Niam Khasi is the monotheistic indigenous faith centred on U Blei Nongthaw, the formless creator, followed by 15.41% of Khasis (2011). The Seng Khasi founding date (1899) is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Jadonang and Rani Gaidinliu's reform of Zeme Naga religion around one god, Tingwang.
trads.an: Founded in the late 1920s by Haipou Jadonang (executed 1931) and led afterward by Rani Gaidinliu; a monotheistic reform of the Zeliangrong Naga faith, worshipping Tingwang exclusively in Kelumki prayer houses; about 25,000–30,000 followers. Start moved from 1930 to 1927.

trads.d: The last surviving Indo-Iranian polytheism. Its gods are Dezau and others, with goat sacrifice, purity rules and seasonal festivals.
trads.an: Animism and ancestor worship with ancient Indo-Iranian, Vedic-like gods (Dezau the creator, Imra, Indr, Mahandeo, Jeṣṭak, Sajigor); goat sacrifice; dehar shamans; strict purity rules (bashaleni); Chilam Joshi, Uchau and Chaumos festivals; 7,466 Kalasha speakers (2023 census).

trads.d: The archaic Indo-Iranian polytheism of Imra and Gish, ended by forced conversion in 1895–96.
trads.an: Neighbouring Nuristanis, who shared a similar archaic faith, were forcibly converted to Islam in 1895–96.

trads.d: Tai worship of phi spirits, guardian spirits and spirit houses alongside Buddhism.
trads.an: Tai folk religion of phi spirits, khwan (vital essences) and ancestors; guardian spirits of temples, towns, villages and houses; miniature spirit shrines; mophi shamans. It blends with Buddhism; about 30% of Lao reportedly follow it, though it is not officially recognized.

trads.d: Worship of the 37 nats, formalized under King Anawrahta in the 11th century: humans deified after death and nature spirits, honoured with possession dances by nat-kadaw mediums.
trads.an: King Anawrahta (1044–1077) formalized the 37 nats under Thagyamin after failing to suppress nat worship. Nats include humans deified after death and nature spirits (not only the 'tragic dead'); nat-kadaw mediums are possessed and dance at nat-pwe festivals alongside Buddhist practice. Taungbyone is not covered by the checked source, so it was removed.

trads.d: Shamans (txiv neeb) heal by recovering lost souls among spirits and ancestors.
trads.an: Shamans (spirit-chosen men or women) heal with ua neeb rites; soul-calling (hu plig) restores lost soul parts; each person has many souls, one of which is reborn; ancestors receive food, spirit money and incense; the household altar (Thaj Neeb).

trads.d: The Tai Ahom kingdom's worship of ancestors and sky gods, revived today.
trads.an: The Ahom form (Ban Phi) with Molung priestly clans.

trads.d: The Vedda people's cult of the dead: ancestral spirits (nae yaku) are invoked for hunting, with the kirikoraha offering and the deity Kande Yakka.
trads.an: A 'cult of the dead': ancestral nae yaku are invoked for hunting, with the kirikoraha offering to the newly dead and a unique deity, Kande Yakka; blended with nominal Buddhism or Hinduism; the Kataragama shrine is shared. Possession and dance are not described in the checked source, so those traits were removed.

trads.d: Böö shamans and ovoo cairns, honoring the Eternal Blue Sky and ancestor spirits. It was revived after 1990.
trads.an: Böö (shaman) from early Mongolian böge; female shamans tied to Etügen, Mother Earth. Ovoo and the post-1990 revival are not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: The revived Sakha faith in the White Creator, with the Ysyakh summer festival.
trads.an: Aar Aiyy Faith dated to 1996, so start moved from 1990 to 1996.

trads.d: The revived 'Tradition of the Old' faith of the Chuvash.
trads.an: Vattisen Yaly listed.

trads.d: Udmurt sacred groves and the god Inmar.
trads.an: Udmurt native religion listed.

trads.d: Modern revivals of pre-Christian Magyar religion.
trads.an: Hungarian native faith listed.

trads.d: Estonian native faith revivals: Taaraism (1928) and Maausk ('earth faith').
trads.an: Taaraism/Maausk listed.

trads.d: Finnish native faith, a 20th-century reconstruction organized as Taivaannaula in 2002. The registered community Karhun kansa gained official minority-religion status in 2013.
trads.an: A 20th-c. reconstruction that gained official minority-religion status in 2013; the registered community Karhun kansa had about 80 members in 2020. Description updated.

trads.d: The Ossetian faith in one god (Xwytsau) and saints such as Uastyrdzhi, descended from Alan religion.
trads.an: Uatsdin listed.

trads.d: Herodotus's account names Tabiti the hearth goddess, Papaios and Api, with sword worship and horse sacrifice.
trads.an: Herodotus names Tabiti (hearth), Papaios (sky father), Api (earth and water), Thagimasadas and Artimpasa; the sword of 'Ares' on a brushwood shrine; horse sacrifice. Of Iranian origin, with possible Ossetian survivals.

trads.d: The Adyghe ethical code and faith in Tha (Thashxwe), revived since the 1990s.
trads.an: Habze listed.

trads.d: A revival of the Armenian pagan gods (Aramazd, Vahagn) based in the temple of Garni.
trads.an: Armenian Hetanism listed.

trads.d: Herodotus describes the Getae's god Zalmoxis, who promised immortality. It ended with the Roman conquest.
trads.an: Herodotus (before 425 BCE) describes the Getae's belief that the dead go to Zalmoxis and the four-yearly messenger sacrifice; the cult's origin is uncertain. The end date (Roman conquest, 106 CE) is not covered by the checked source.

trads.d: Aurelian made the 'Unconquered Sun' a chief official god in 274.
trads.an: Aurelian made Sol Invictus a chief imperial god with a temple dedicated 25 December 274; the last known inscription is from 387.

trads.d: Victor Anderson's (1917–2001) ecstatic witchcraft.
trads.an: Feri tradition listed; year from standard references.

trads.d: Zsuzsanna Budapest's women-only Goddess worship.
trads.an: Dianic Wicca listed; year from standard references.
kt: The Holy Book of Women's Mysteries

trads.d: Starhawk's activist witchcraft tradition.
trads.an: Reclaiming listed; year from standard references.

trads.d: A neo-pagan church inspired by Heinlein's 'Stranger in a Strange Land'.
trads.an: Church of All Worlds listed; year from standard references.

trads.d: Franz Anton Mesmer's (1734–1814) 'animal magnetism', a forerunner of Spiritualism and New Thought.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Christian esotericism from Martinès de Pasqually and Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, organized as an order in 1891.
trads.an: Martinès de Pasqually founded the Élus Coëns in 1765; Saint-Martin's inward 'Way of the Heart'; Papus and Chaboseau organized the Martinist Order in the 1880s–1891; Christian esotericism of reintegration.
kt: Treatise on the Reintegration of Beings

trads.d: Pico della Mirandola and Reuchlin read Kabbalah as confirming Christianity.
trads.an: A Renaissance reinterpretation of Kabbalah through the Trinity, led by Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) and Reuchlin (1455–1522), with later figures such as Kircher and Knorr von Rosenroth; faded by about 1750 and persisted in occultism. End moved from 1700 to 1750.

trads.d: Max Heindel's (1865–1919) Christian esoteric school.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: The Rosicrucian Order AMORC of H. Spencer Lewis, taught by correspondence.
trads.an: Founded 1915 by Harvey Spencer Lewis; correspondence lessons; headquarters in San Jose; about 250,000 members reported in 1990.

trads.d: An initiatory order that adopted Crowley's Thelema in the 1910s.
trads.an: Apparently founded by Carl Kellner, with Theodor Reuss; nothing verifiable about it before 1904. Crowley joined in 1910, headed the British section in 1912 and made Thelema its guiding philosophy; Outer Head from 1925. The Gnostic Mass (Liber XV) dates from 1913.

trads.d: Alice Bailey's teachings, attributed to a Master called 'the Tibetan', which shaped the New Age.
trads.an: Arcane School founded in 1923 by Alice and Foster Bailey (part of the Lucis Trust). Bailey said her works were dictated by 'the Tibetan' (Djwal Khul), and she is often credited with popularizing the term 'New Age'.
kt: A Treatise on the Seven Rays

trads.d: Guy Ballard's (1878–1939) Ascended Master teachings.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Mark and Elizabeth Clare Prophet's Summit Lighthouse (1958), whose followers sheltered against nuclear war in Montana in 1990.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Nicholas and Helena Roerich's 'Living Ethics'.
trads.an: Agni Yoga Society founded in 1920 by Nicholas and Helena Roerich; 'Living Ethics' or the Teaching of Life, presented as transmitted by Master Morya; a Neo-Theosophical teaching.

trads.d: G. I. Gurdjieff's 'work' of self-remembering and sacred dances.
trads.an: Gurdjieff's Fourth Way, or 'The Work', with the Movements sacred dances, the idea of humans living in 'waking sleep', and Ouspensky's In Search of the Miraculous. The 1912 Moscow start date is not confirmed by this source; the travels ran c. 1890–1912.

trads.d: Peter Deunov's esoteric Christianity, with paneurhythmy dance and an August pilgrimage to the Rila Mountains.
trads.an: Peter Deunov founded the movement in Bulgaria in 1897 (start moved from 1900). Esoteric Christianity; paneurhythmy developed from the 1930s, with an August pilgrimage to the Rila Mountains; Omraam Mikhaël Aïvanhov brought it to France in 1937. The sunrise prayer is not covered by this source.

trads.d: Ernest and Ruth Norman's (1900–1993) teaching of past lives and awaited 'Space Brothers'.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: George King's movement, which received teachings from 'Cosmic Masters' on other planets.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Marshall Applewhite and Bonnie Nettles' UFO movement. It ended with the mass suicide of its members in 1997.
trads.an: Founded 1974 by Marshall Applewhite ('Do') and Bonnie Nettles ('Ti'). It mixed Christian millenarianism, New Age ideas and ufology. In March 1997, 39 members died in a mass suicide timed to Comet Hale–Bopp, at Rancho Santa Fe.

trads.d: Samael Aun Weor's (1917–1977) neo-Gnostic teachings.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Founded on Edgar Cayce's (1877–1945) trance readings.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Ernest Holmes's (1887–1960) 'Science of Mind'.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Charles and Myrtle Fillmore's Christian New Thought.
trads.an: Charles and Myrtle Fillmore began publishing Modern Thought in Kansas City in 1889. It is the largest New Thought body and the only one with a significant Christian identity. Unity Village; Silent Unity prayer ministry; Daily Word since 1924.

trads.d: John Newbrough's (1828–1891) channeled bible, 'Oahspe'.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Michael Harner's 'core shamanism' and related Western revivals.
trads.an: Grew out of the late-20th-century counterculture: Eliade (1951) and Castaneda (1968, now widely regarded as fiction). Harner's 'core shamanism' (The Way of the Shaman, 1980) is the most widely used system. Native scholars criticize it as appropriation ('plastic shamans').

trads.d: Michael Aquino's split from the Church of Satan, which treats Set as a real principle of self-deification.
trads.an: Founded 1975 in San Francisco by Michael Aquino, who left the Church of Satan. Set is a real entity, revered as a model rather than worshipped; Xeper ('becoming') aims at self-deification. About 500 members by estimate.
kt: The Book of Coming Forth by Night

trads.d: Pragmatic magic in which belief itself is a tool.
trads.an: Emerged in 1970s England with Peter Carroll and Ray Sherwin; the Illuminates of Thanateros were announced 1976–77, and Liber Null was published in 1978. Austin Osman Spare is its 'grandfather'. Belief is treated as a tool.

trads.d: A parody religion of Eris, goddess of chaos, from the 'Principia Discordia'.
trads.an: Founded by Greg Hill (Malaclypse the Younger) and Kerry Thornley (Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst). The Principia Discordia was first printed in 1963, with later editions in 1965 and 1970; centred on Eris. It began as a joke, and scholars now see genuine religious meaning for many adherents.

trads.d: A revolutionary atheistic cult of Reason (Momoro, 1756–1794) in Notre-Dame.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Robespierre's (1758–1794) deist state cult, which lasted months.
trads.an: Name and founder or date confirmed in the cited list.

trads.d: Chemin-Dupontès' (1760–1852) deist congregations.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Auguste Comte's (1798–1857) worship of Humanity. Positivist temples survive in Brazil.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.

trads.d: Secular congregations with songs and talks.
trads.an: Founded January 2013 in London by Sanderson Jones and Pippa Evans; 48 locations as of 2019, and assemblies have met in about 90 cities over time.

trads.d: Isak Gerson's church, for which copying information is sacred. Sweden recognized it in 2012.
trads.an: Name (and founder where given) confirmed in the cited list; the date follows standard references and is not confirmed there.
